title: Bridging Stochastic Flow Maps and Boltzmann Generators with Normalizing Flows

paper.title: Bridging Stochastic Flow Maps and Boltzmann Generators with Normalizing Flows
paper.abstract: Abstract Generating independent, equilibrium samples of molecular systems at scale remains a central obstacle in computational statistical mechanics. Boltzmann Generators address this by pairing a generative model with importance sampling to obtain consistent samples from the target distribution. We introduce Normalizing Flow Flow Maps (NF 2 M), which combines the strengths of recent stochastic flow maps with the tractability of classic normalizing flows to build a Boltzmann Generator. Unlike most methods, which correct the generative model only at the end, NF 2 M reweighs each denoising transition as generation proceeds, avoiding wasted compute on trajectories that are ultimately discarded. At each denoising step, a conditional normalizing flow proposes clean configurations given the current noisy state (a simpler task than sampling directly from the target) and its exact likelihood enables correcting each proposal toward the true denoising transition of the target Boltzmann distribution. This is in contrast to most existing methods, whose likelihoods are approximate or expensive to evaluate, undermining the statistical reliability of the correction. We establish consistency of the corrected transitions and bound how approximation errors propagate through the sampling chain. We evaluate NF 2 M on peptide systems, demonstrating improved sampling efficiency and sample quality.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Sampling the Boltzmann distribution of molecular systems is central to statistical physics, underlying protein folding, ligand binding, conformational change, and molecular design ( Liu, 2001 ; Frenkel and Smit, 2001 ; Noé et al., 2009 ; Lindorff-Larsen et al., 2011 ; Buch et al., 2011 ) . This remains hard because molecular energy landscapes are high-dimensional and rugged, with metastable states separated by large barriers. Classical approaches like MD and MCMC are asymptotically exact ( Leimkuhler and Matthews, 2015 ; Frenkel and Smit, 2001 ; Wirnsberger et al., 2020 ) , but their local-update nature makes them mix slowly on such landscapes, producing correlated samples and requiring prohibitively long runs to capture transitions between metastable states. Boltzmann Generators (BGs) take a different strategy ( Noé et al., 2019 ; Müller et al., 2019 ) : a learned generative model produces plausible configurations independently and in parallel, which are then statistically corrected toward the true equilibrium distribution, e.g. via importance sampling (IS). This hinges on two requirements: proposal-target overlap and a tractable correction procedure—that existing generative backbones trade off differently. Normalizing flows (NFs) ( Rezende and Mohamed, 2015 ; Dinh et al., 2017 ; Noé et al., 2019 ; Papamakarios et al., 2021 ) dominate this role because their tractable likelihoods enable IS correction, but their invertibility constraints limit expressiveness and overlap. Bridging the NF to target gap via temperature-annealed interpolation ( Tan et al., 2025 ) instead suffers from mass teleportation on multimodal targets ( Woodard et al., 2009 ; Máté and Fleuret, 2023 ) and does not reliably outperform direct importance sampling ( Tan et al., 2025 ) . Continuous normalizing flows built from ODE trajectories ( Chen et al., 2018 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ) offer more expressive architectures, but their likelihoods require integrating the vector-field divergence, making correction costly and discretization-sensitive. Distilling these into few-step flow maps ( Boffi et al., 2025 ) sacrifices tractable likelihoods altogether. Subsequent work restores likelihoods for such few-step maps in two ways : FALCON ( Rehman et al., 2026a ) computes them from the full Jacobian of the map, at the cost of memory overhead and sensitivity to the map’s numerical invertibility, while F2D2 ( Ai et al., 2026 ) and SCALLOP ( OuYang et al., 2026 ) instead distill a likelihood-prediction head, gaining speed but risking error propagation from the learned likelihood into the correction step. Diffusion models offer a different stochastic transport path, gradually perturbing clean samples via a tractable noising process and generating through learned, typically Gaussian, denoising transitions ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) . These paths handle multimodal targets better than temperature annealing and have shown promise for BGs ( Grenioux and Noble, 2026 ) : although the endpoint density is intractable, the path density can be evaluated, enabling correction in an extended space ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . The Gaussian approximation is accurate only for fine discretizations, however, creating a tradeoff between statistical performance and inference cost ( Grenioux and Noble, 2026 ) . Distributional diffusion and stochastic flow maps address this by modeling the full conditional distribution of clean samples given a noisy state, enabling expressive transitions over larger stepsizes ( De Bortoli et al., 2025 ; Potaptchik et al., 2026 ; Holderrieth et al., 2026 ) but the resulting models are typically implicit, lacking the likelihoods BG correction needs. We close this gap with Normalizing Flow Flow Maps (NF 2 M), a BG that generates samples along a diffusion transport path in a few steps using denoising kernels estimated via importance sampling. Like stochastic flow maps, NF 2 M models the conditional distribution q θ ​ ( x 0 | x t ) q^{\theta}(x_{0}|x_{t}) of clean data given a noisy state, but it uses a conditional NF rather than an implicit model, yielding a tractable density. This tractability lets us build an importance-sampling estimator of the true denoising kernel, exact as the number of particles grows: at each step, we propose candidates from q θ ​ ( x 0 | x t ) q^{\theta}(x_{0}|x_{t}) and reweight them against the tractable conditional target p ⁡ ( x 0 | x t ) p(x_{0}|x_{t}) (which is the product of the Boltzmann density and the diffusion noising kernel) yielding a Rao-Blackwellized mixture estimator that we sample to denoise the current state. Iterating this gradually transports noise toward the Boltzmann target, unlike NF- and CNF-based BGs that bridge the gap in one step. By stochastic localization ( Grenioux et al., 2024 ) , p ⁡ ( x 0 | x t ) p(x_{0}|x_{t}) loses its multimodality and concentrates as t → 0 t\to 0 which makes it easier to sample from and simplifies the conditional NF’s approximation target. Our main contributions are: • We propose Normalizing Flow Flow Maps (NF 2 M), a Boltzmann Generator that parameterizes a stochastic flow map with a normalizing flow, combining tractable densities with few-step generation. • We design novel conditional normalizing flow architectures for molecule generation, adapting state-of-the-art image and video normalizing flows to this setting ( Zhai et al., 2025 ; Gu et al., 2026 ) . • We propose two inference strategies, NF 2 M-IS and NF 2 M-MIS, that yield asymptotically exact samples from the Boltzmann distribution, and support them with theoretical guarantees. • We evaluate NF 2 M against NF and flow-map baselines across molecular systems of varying sizes, demonstrating competitive or superior performance.

sections.heading: Boltzmann Generators.
sections.text: Boltzmann Generators (BGs) ( Noé et al., 2019 ; Müller et al., 2019 ) use a learned model q θ q^{\theta} to propose configurations and then correct its mismatch with the Boltzmann target by self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS) . Given M M independent proposals x m ∼ q θ x^{m}\sim q^{\theta} , the unnormalized weights and estimator of an observable 𝒪 \mathcal{O} are w ~ m = exp ⁡ { − ℰ ⁡ ( x m ) } q θ ​ ( x m ) , 𝔼 ^ p ​ [ 𝒪 ] = ∑ m = 1 M w ~ m ​ 𝒪 ​ ( x m ) ∑ m = 1 M w ~ m . \widetilde{w}^{m}=\frac{\exp\{-\mathcal{E}(x^{m})\}}{q^{\theta}(x^{m})},\qquad\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{p}[\mathcal{O}]=\frac{\sum_{m=1}^{M}\widetilde{w}^{m}\mathcal{O}(x^{m})}{\sum_{m=1}^{M}\widetilde{w}^{m}}. (2) The estimator is generally biased at finite M M but is consistent as M → ∞ M\to\infty , provided the proposal’s support covers the target’s. Its variance depends on the overlap between q θ q^{\theta} and p p , and computing the importance weights requires evaluating the proposal density q θ ​ ( x ) q^{\theta}(x) .

sections.heading: Normalizing flows.
sections.text: Normalizing flows (NFs) ( Rezende and Mohamed, 2015 ; Dinh et al., 2017 ) are a natural choice for parameterizing q θ q^{\theta} because they support both sampling and exact density evaluation. A NF learns a diffeomorphism T θ : ℝ d → ℝ d \mathrm{T}_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} from data to a base density ρ \rho , typically 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) , so that T θ − 1 \mathrm{T}_{\theta}^{-1} maps base samples to data space. Its density follows from the change-of-variables formula, log ⁡ q θ ​ ( x ) = log ⁡ ρ ⁡ ( T θ ​ ( x ) ) + log ⁡ | det ⁡ ∂ T θ ​ ( x ) ∂ x | . \log q^{\theta}(x)=\log\rho(\mathrm{T}_{\theta}(x))+\log\absolutevalue{\det\frac{\partial\mathrm{T}_\theta(x)}{\partial x}}. (3) In practice, T θ \mathrm{T}_{\theta} is a composition of invertible layers whose inverses and Jacobian determinants are tractable. These structural requirements enable exact likelihoods but constrain the neural-network architectures that can be used, thereby limiting the expressivity of the learned distribution.

sections.heading: 3 Normalizing Flow Flow Maps (NF 2 M)
sections.text: Figure 1: Conceptual illustration of the NF 2 M mechanism. Given a sample x t x_{t} drawn from the marginal distribution at noise level t t , we first draw M M samples { x 0 | t m } m = 1 M \{x_{0|t}^{m}\}_{m=1}^{M} from the learned posterior q 0 | t θ ( ⋅ | x t ) q_{0|t}^{\theta}(\cdot|x_{t}) . We then reweight them via Eq. 12 to construct the posterior p s | t θ , M p_{s|t}^{\theta,M} , which proposes a sample x s x_{s} at the next noise level s s . We repeat this procedure until reaching the target distribution. While existing BG designs compose approximate transitions and correct accumulated error only at the end by reweighting the full composition, NF 2 M instead reweighs each denoising transition directly along the diffusion path of Sec. 2 , with target p 0 = p p_{0}=p . Since each transition is individually asymptotically unbiased, so is their composition, with no need for a final correction. Concretely, NF 2 M learns a conditional normalizing flow q 0 | t θ ​ ( x 0 | x t ) q^{\theta}_{0|t}(x_{0}|x_{t}) approximating the denoising posterior at every noise level: the flow proposes clean configurations from the current noisy state, importance sampling corrects them toward the true posterior, and the result determines the transition via Eq. 7 . Sec. 3.1 describes the basic sampler, NF 2 M-IS; Sec. 3.2 covers its training objective and flow architecture; Sec. 3.3 improves inference through a trajectory-sharing mechanism and a custom MCMC scheme; and Sec. 3.4 provides theoretical intuition and guarantees.

sections.heading: 3.2 Training
sections.text: We now discuss how to train the conditional flow q 0 | t θ q^{\theta}_{0|t} . Although equilibrium samples from the Boltzmann target p p are unavailable, we have access to a biased dataset 𝒟 \mathcal{D} drawn from some distribution q := q 0 q:=q_{0} . Applying the same forward noising process to q 0 q_{0} induces a noisy marginal q t q_{t} and denoising posterior q 0 | t q_{0|t} , and we train q 0 | t θ q^{\theta}_{0|t} to approximate q 0 | t q_{0|t} from noisy–clean pairs generated from 𝒟 \mathcal{D} . The bias inherited from 𝒟 \mathcal{D} is corrected only later, at inference time.

sections.heading: Conditional Normalizing Flow architecture.
sections.text: We develop conditional molecular variants of TarFlow ( Zhai et al., 2025 ) and StarFlow ( Gu et al., 2026 ) . Both are autoregressive flows ( Huang et al., 2018 ) that use causal Transformers for autoregressive affine coupling, giving a triangular Jacobian that enables parallel density evaluation with sequential sampling. TarFlow stacks several medium conditioned blocks while StarFlow uses one large conditional block followed by small unconditional ones. Following Tan et al. (2025) , we represent an N N -atom configuration as N N tokens in ℝ 3 \mathbb{R}^{3} , conditioning both backbones on noise level t t (via DiT-style adaptive layer norm ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) ) and on x t x_{t} itself, either through cross-attention (features of x 0 x_{0} as queries, x t x_{t} as keys/values) or a prefix mechanism (prepending x t x_{t} features to the autoregressive sequence). Details in Sec. A.5 .

sections.heading: Molecular symmetries.
sections.text: Following Tan et al. (2025) , we enforce translation and rotation invariance by centering and randomly rotating configurations rather than using equivariance. We lift them to ℝ N × 3 \mathbb{R}^{N\times 3} with a Gaussian centroid c 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , N − 1 ​ I 3 ) c_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,N^{-1}I_{3}) , tractable under a standard Gaussian base. To reduce centroid-induced importance-weight variance, a closed-form adjustment to log ⁡ q 0 | t θ ​ ( x 0 | x t ) \log q^{\theta}_{0|t}(x_{0}|x_{t}) removes the rotationally irrelevant angular component of the centroid’s offset from its conditional mean given x t x_{t} . This recovers Tan et al. (2025) ’s unconditional correction at high noise ( Sec. A.4 ).

sections.text: NF 2 M-IS shares candidates only at initialization. Can this sharing be extended further along the chain? When p p is a Gaussian 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ , γ 2 ​ I d ) \mathcal{N}(\mu,\gamma^{2}\mathrm{I}_{d}) , one can show that 𝔻 KL ( p 0 | t ( ⋅ ∣ x ) ∥ p 0 | t ( ⋅ ∣ y ) ) = α t 2 ​ γ 2 ​ ‖ x − y ‖ 2 2 ​ σ t 2 ​ ( α t 2 ​ γ 2 + σ t 2 ) , ∀ x , y ∈ ℝ d , t ∈ [ 0 , T ] . \displaystyle\mathbb{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{0|t}(\cdot\mid x)~\|~p_{0|t}(\cdot\mid y))=\frac{\alpha_{t}^{2}\gamma^{2}\norm{x-y}^{2}}{2\sigma_{t}^{2}(\alpha_{t}^{2}\gamma^{2}+\sigma_{t}^{2})},\forall x,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d},t\in[0,T]. (17) Posteriors conditioned on nearby states are themselves close, which suggests a simple idea: when x x and y y are close, candidates drawn from q 0 | t θ ( ⋅ | x ) q^{\theta}_{0|t}(\cdot|x) should also be informative proposals for p 0 | t ( ⋅ | y ) p_{0|t}(\cdot|y) . This is exactly the idea behind NF 2 M-MIS : each trajectory reuses candidates generated for other trajectories, rather than drawing its own ( Fig. 3 ). Concretely, instead of keeping the M M candidates from each of N N proposals separate, we pool them into N N groups of C C shared proposal components, so that each trajectory draws on C ​ M CM candidates rather than M M , for the same total of N ​ M NM flow samples as NF 2 M-IS. This comes at the cost of evaluating additional cross-likelihoods for the importance weights, an overhead that remains comparatively inexpensive for our autoregressive flow architectures. Such sharing is especially valuable at high noise levels, where noisy states are less informative about x 0 x_{0} and the posterior across trajectories approach the common Boltzmann target. follows literature on multiple importance sampling ( Veach and Guibas, 1995 ; Owen and Zhou, 2000 ; He and Owen, 2014 ; Bugallo et al., 2017 ; Elvira et al., 2019 ) . See Sec. A.2 for algorithmic details.

sections.text: Why approximate the denoising posterior at intermediate noise levels instead of applying SNIS directly to the final Boltzmann target? The following proposition quantifies how the endpoint-conditioned Gaussian transition controls this error; its proof is given in Sec. A.1 . Then W ℓ ( p s | t ( ⋅ ∣ x t ) , p ^ s | t ( ⋅ ∣ x t ) ) ≤ a s , t W ℓ ( p 0 | t ( ⋅ ∣ x t ) , p ^ 0 | t ( ⋅ ∣ x t ) ) . \displaystyle W_{\ell}\left(p_{s|t}(\cdot\mid x_{t}),\,\hat{p}_{s|t}(\cdot\mid x_{t})\right)\leq a_{s,t}\,W_{\ell}\left(p_{0|t}(\cdot\mid x_{t}),\,\hat{p}_{0|t}(\cdot\mid x_{t})\right).

sections.heading: BGs with tractable correction weights.
sections.text: Sequential Boltzmann Generators (SBG) use sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) to sample along a geometric annealing path between a trained TarFlow proposal and the Boltzmann target. However, their ablation results show that SMC does not consistently improve over SNIS on the same trained proposal across systems and metrics ( Tan et al., 2025 ) . NF 2 M also deploys a TarFlow sequentially, but both inference and learning differ fundamentally: rather than annealing a fixed proposal toward the target, NF 2 M performs progressive denoising transitions, and the flow itself is trained as a conditional model rather than an unconditional one. The Autoregressive Boltzmann Generator (ArBG) models coordinate-bin probabilities with uniform dequantization ( Rehman et al., 2026b ) , yielding an exactly evaluable but bin-wise coarse density. Its coordinate-wise factorization enables twisted SMC using temporarily capped peptide energies to resample partial structures. Stochastic normalizing flows interleave invertible maps with MCMC or Langevin transitions, weighting entire sampling paths ( Wu et al., 2020 ) . NF 2 M instead corrects denoising proposals over complete molecular configurations at each noise level, avoiding both the binning artifacts of ArBG and the need to evaluate energies of artificially capped partial structures.

sections.heading: BGs with approximate correction.
sections.text: Free-form Flows jointly train a network and its pseudo-inverse by maximum likelihood ( Draxler et al., 2024 ) . Continuous normalizing flows keep maximum-likelihood training but replace the invertible network with a neural ODE ( Köhler et al., 2020 ) , whose likelihood requires integrating the costly probability-flow ODE through the network’s divergence, with many steps needed for both accuracy and invertibility. Later work cuts training cost via flow matching but leaves this inference cost untouched ( Klein et al., 2023b ; Klein and Noé, 2024 ) . FALCON instead distills into a few-step flow map, replacing the full ODE integration with a handful of Jacobian evaluations, at the price of only approximate invertibility ( Rehman et al., 2026a ) . F2D2 drops exact Jacobians entirely, jointly distilling the flow map and its density evolution via Hutchinson trace estimates ( Ai et al., 2026 ; Hutchinson, 1990 ) , and SCALLOP replaces this with a Hutchinson-free conditional divergence-matching loss ( OuYang et al., 2026 ) . Across these distillation-based methods, the learned density’s approximation error enters the importance weights directly and persists regardless of proposal count. NF 2 M instead evaluates its conditional proposal densities exactly.

sections.heading: Stochastic flow maps and intermediate correction.
sections.text: Distributional diffusion models learn the conditional distribution of clean states given noisy states, enabling larger denoising steps ( Xiao et al., 2022 ; De Bortoli et al., 2025 ) . Meta Flow Maps and Diamond Maps use clean-state candidates for intermediate correction toward reward-tilted distributions ( Potaptchik et al., 2026 ; Holderrieth et al., 2026 ) . Their implicit conditional generators do not directly provide the proposal densities needed for Boltzmann importance weights. NF 2 M supplies them through a conditional normalizing flow.

sections.heading: Benchmarks.
sections.text: We evaluate on the five all-atom peptide systems of Tan et al. (2025) reusing their MD training trajectories, splits, force fields, and evaluation protocol throughout so our numbers are directly comparable to theirs. We report the energy Wasserstein distance ( ℰ ​ - ​ 𝒲 2 \mathcal{E}\text{-}\mathcal{W}_{2} , sensitive to fine local structure) and the dihedral torus Wasserstein distance ( 𝕋 ​ - ​ 𝒲 2 \mathbb{T}\text{-}\mathcal{W}_{2} , sensitive to metastable-state occupancy), each against 10 4 10^{4} held-out reference configurations over three seeds ( Sec. B.1 ).

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare NF 2 M (variants NF 2 M-IS and NF 2 M-MIS) against SNIS, the exact-Jacobian flow maps FALCON and FALCON-A ( Rehman et al., 2026a ) , and the distilled-density flow maps F2D2 ( Ai et al., 2026 ) and SCALLOP ( OuYang et al., 2026 ) . The flow-maps are distilled from the same per-system velocity teacher, which uses a DiT-style backbone ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) . Our SNIS baseline applies direct self-normalized importance sampling to an unconditional molecular flow proposal trained following Tan et al. (2025) , without their annealed SMC procedure. We additionally compare against the NF-based SMC sampler from Tan et al. (2025) in Tab. 26 : it does not consistently outperform the cheaper direct-SNIS baseline, which we retain in the main comparison. For each system, their total wall-clock training budget, including the teacher and flow-map pretraining, matches the training time of the selected NF 2 M checkpoint ( Sec. B.2 ).

sections.heading: Budgets.
sections.text: Proposal budgets otherwise follow each method’s practical operating point: NF 2 M draws its final 10 4 10^{4} particles directly, while SNIS and the four flow-map baselines first draw 10 6 10^{6} proposals and then resample 10 4 10^{4} samples for evaluation (except FALCON/FALCON-A on chignolin, where exact per-step Jacobian costs cap the pool at 10 5 10^{5} ). For NF 2 M, we run 512 MAExL steps followed by 128 post-hoc MALA steps targeting the Boltzmann distribution. For all other methods, we apply enough post-hoc MALA steps to the final 10 4 10^{4} samples to match NF 2 M’s total target-energy evaluations; all metrics use 10 4 10^{4} final samples. Tab. 23 compares the cost of this refinement to the total cost of each method, and Tab. 25 reports the number of post-hoc MALA steps used for each method.

On the smallest systems ALA-2/ALA-3, SNIS achieves the lowest 𝕋 ​ - ​ 𝒲 2 \mathbb{T}\text{-}\mathcal{W}_{2} , reflecting the closest match to the reference dihedral-angle distribution. However, SNIS’s 𝕋 ​ - ​ 𝒲 2 \mathbb{T}\text{-}\mathcal{W}_{2} rises on the larger systems. In contrast, NF 2 M’s progressive correction maintains stronger performance, achieving the lowest 𝕋 \mathbb{T} - 𝒲 2 \mathcal{W}_{2} on the largest systems, ALA-6 and chignolin, with FALCON and FALCON-A in between. FALCON achieves the lowest ℰ \mathcal{E} - 𝒲 2 \mathcal{W}_{2} on ALA-6, where NF 2 M does not lead on that metric. F2D2 and SCALLOP have substantially higher ℰ \mathcal{E} - 𝒲 2 \mathcal{W}_{2} on ALA-4 and ALA-6. We also ablate NF 2 M’s in-loop MAExL: it improves energy accuracy and stability with little change in torsion distances, while increasing from 512 to 1024 steps brings little further benefit for IS ( Tab. 4 ). Separately, removing post-hoc MALA from all methods changes NF 2 M’s results relatively little but substantially worsens energy accuracy for several baselines ( Tab. 24 ). sections.heading: The accuracy-efficiency trade-off of flow-map methods.
sections.text: Tab. 2 shows that NF 2 M-IS/MIS have comparable training and inference time to SNIS, although they require more training time on chignolin. FALCON, F2D2, and SCALLOP use different approximations of proposal densities, resulting in distinct accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs. F2D2 and SCALLOP predict density changes with a learned divergence head, with inference times comparable to NF 2 M and SNIS on the ALA systems while roughly 1.6–2x slower on chignolin. FALCONs instead compute full flow-map Jacobians; without guaranteed invertibility, their determinants need not yield exact proposal densities.Their inference is roughly 11 × 11\times slower than SNIS on ALA-2 and 48 48 – 129 × 129\times slower on ALA-3 through ALA-6. On chignolin, a full 10 6 10^{6} -proposal evaluation was projected at ∼ 500 \sim 500 GPU-hours per seed ( Sec. B.2.2 ), forcing a reduced pool of 10 5 10^{5} — still ∼ 60 × \sim 60\times slower than SNIS or NF 2 M-IS. We additionally show that under SNIS, distilled flow maps do not consistently outperform their velocity teacher ( Tab. 22 ).By contrast, NF 2 M computes its conditional proposal density exactly from the flow’s tractable Jacobian.

sections.heading: NF 2 M: IS versus MIS.
sections.text: NF 2 M-IS and NF 2 M-MIS perform similarly, with MIS using a smaller candidate budget. MIS reduces inference time most clearly on chignolin, with smaller differences on ALA systems. At matched candidate budgets, IS and MIS achieve comparable inner ESS, although both exhibit substantial weight concentration at low noise, especially on chignolin ( Fig. 4 ). Overall, NF 2 M delivers strong performance at comparable training cost. Its inference time is broadly comparable to SNIS, F2D2, and SCALLOP and much shorter than FALCON and FALCON-A. Its performance advantage is most pronounced on the larger systems.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented NF 2 M, a Boltzmann Generator that parameterizes a stochastic flow map with a conditional normalizing flow, correcting each denoising transition via tractable SNIS. This yields consistent samples with theoretical error control and strong empirical performance across peptide systems, with no approximate likelihood. Currently, NF 2 M is trained per system; a natural next step is transferability across peptides as in Tan et al. (2025) , learning a single conditional flow that generalizes across sequences and lengths. One other promising directions would be to do training with the reverse KL in Sec. 3.2 to further refining the model.

sections.text: Compared with the non-rejuvenated SNIS bound of Thm. 7 , the leading oscillation term is multiplied by the MAExL mixing factor C t ​ r t L ​ V t , u C_{t}\,r_{t}^{L}\,V_{t,u} . sections.heading: A.2 Multiple Importance Sampling
sections.text: This appendix details the NF 2 M-MIS sampler introduced in Sec. 3.3 , which builds on the multiple importance sampling (MIS) literature ( Veach and Guibas, 1995 ; Owen and Zhou, 2000 ; He and Owen, 2014 ; Bugallo et al., 2017 ; Elvira et al., 2019 ) . Recall that NF 2 M-IS shares candidates only at initialization; the KL identity ( 17 ) is what lets us extend this sharing further along the chain, since it shows that posteriors conditioned on nearby noisy states are themselves close. We specify the mixture proposal, component selection, and candidate sharing; derive the self-normalized importance-sampling correction for the reverse kernel; and give the full algorithm together with its computational cost.

sections.heading: Mixture proposal.
sections.text: At noise level t t , let { x t i } i = 1 N \{x_{t}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} denote the current trajectories. For each trajectory i i , we build a mixture proposal by combining C C selected learned posteriors, m 0 | t θ ​ ( x 0 ∣ x t i ) = ∑ c ∈ 𝒞 ⁡ ( i ) ω i , c ​ q 0 | t θ ​ ( x 0 ∣ x t c ) , ∑ c ∈ 𝒞 ⁡ ( i ) ω i , c = 1 , m^{\theta}_{0|t}(x_{0}\mid x_{t}^{i})=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}(i)}\omega_{i,c}\,q^{\theta}_{0|t}\left(x_{0}\mid x_{t}^{c}\right),\qquad\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}(i)}\omega_{i,c}=1, (52) while keeping the target unchanged at p 0 | t ( ⋅ | x t i ) p_{0|t}(\cdot|x_{t}^{i}) . The component set 𝒞 ⁡ ( i ) \mathcal{C}(i) is a multiset of trajectory indices that always contains i i itself, so trajectory i i ’s own posterior is always a summand; the other C − 1 C-1 slots are drawn from elsewhere in the ensemble. Fig. 3 works through a small example of this construction and of the candidate sharing described below. x t 1 x_{t}^{1} source j = 1 j=1 draw M M x 0 1 , 1 x_{0}^{1,1} x 0 1 , 2 x_{0}^{1,2} x 0 1 , 3 x_{0}^{1,3} x t 2 x_{t}^{2} source j = 2 j=2 draw M M x 0 2 , 1 x_{0}^{2,1} x 0 2 , 2 x_{0}^{2,2} x 0 2 , 3 x_{0}^{2,3} x t 3 x_{t}^{3} source j = 3 j=3 draw M M x 0 3 , 1 x_{0}^{3,1} x 0 3 , 2 x_{0}^{3,2} x 0 3 , 3 x_{0}^{3,3} receiving trajectory i = 1 i=1 m 0 | t θ ( ⋅ ∣ x t 1 ) m^{\theta}_{0|t}(\cdot\mid x_{t}^{1}) receiving trajectory i = 2 i=2 m 0 | t θ ( ⋅ ∣ x t 2 ) m^{\theta}_{0|t}(\cdot\mid x_{t}^{2}) c = 1 c=1 (own) c = 2 c=2 c = 2 c=2 (own) c = 3 c=3 x s 1 x_{s}^{1} x s 2 x_{s}^{2} weights Ω 1 , c , m \Omega_{1,c,m} select ( c , m ) (c,m) ; Gaussian transition weights Ω 2 , c , m \Omega_{2,c,m} select ( c , m ) (c,m) ; Gaussian transition Figure 3: Candidate sharing and indexing in NF 2 M-MIS. The example uses N = 3 N=3 sources, M = 3 M=3 candidates per source, and C = 2 C=2 components per mixture; two receiving trajectories are shown. Candidate x 0 j , m x_{0}^{j,m} is indexed by its source j j and position m m within that source’s batch. For receiving trajectory i i , a component c ∈ 𝒞 ⁡ ( i ) c\in\mathcal{C}(i) is itself a source index: c = i c=i always appears (the trajectory’s “own” component), and the remaining slots are drawn by posterior proximity. The middle batch, drawn once from source j = 2 j=2 , is reused by both trajectories: it serves as component c = 2 c=2 of trajectory 1 1 ’s mixture and as the own component c = 2 c=2 of trajectory 2 2 ’s mixture, receiving weight Ω 1 , 2 , m \Omega_{1,2,m} and Ω 2 , 2 , m \Omega_{2,2,m} respectively — the same M M flow draws inform two different reverse steps. Each trajectory samples ( c , m ) (c,m) from its own categorical weights and applies the endpoint-conditioned Gaussian transition. When a source is selected more than once within the same mixture, the repeat instead draws a fresh, independent batch, indexed by the occurrence counter r ⁡ ( i , c ) r(i,c) introduced below.

sections.heading: Choosing components by posterior proximity.
sections.text: By ( 17 ), for a Gaussian target 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ , γ 2 ​ I d ) \mathcal{N}(\mu,\gamma^{2}\mathrm{I}_{d}) the denoising posteriors satisfy KL ( p 0 | t ( ⋅ ∣ x ) ∥ p 0 | t ( ⋅ ∣ y ) ) = β t ‖ x − y ‖ 2 , β t = α t 2 ​ γ 2 2 ​ σ t 2 ​ ( α t 2 ​ γ 2 + σ t 2 ) , \displaystyle\operatorname{KL}\left(p_{0|t}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,p_{0|t}(\cdot\mid y)\right)=\beta_{t}\norm{x-y}^{2},\qquad\beta_{t}=\frac{\alpha_{t}^{2}\gamma^{2}}{2\sigma_{t}^{2}(\alpha_{t}^{2}\gamma^{2}+\sigma_{t}^{2})}, so state-space distance provides a schedule-dependent measure of posterior similarity in this Gaussian case; for molecular targets we use it as a heuristic with γ 2 = 1 \gamma^{2}=1 in normalized coordinates. This is also what makes sharing most valuable at high noise levels: as t t grows, β t → 0 \beta_{t}\to 0 and the bound above shows the posteriors across all trajectories converge toward the common Boltzmann target, so nearly any component is an informative proposal for any trajectory. Given β t \beta_{t} , define for every pair ( i , j ) (i,j) the proximity score λ j ​ ( i ) = exp ⁡ { − β t ​ ‖ x t i − x t j ‖ 2 } . \lambda_{j}(i)=\exp\left\{-\beta_{t}\norm{x_t^i - x_t^j}^{2}\right\}. (53) The component set 𝒞 ⁡ ( i ) \mathcal{C}(i) always retains the slot i i itself, and the remaining C − 1 C-1 slots are drawn independently, with replacement, from the multinomial over { 1 , … , N } \{1,\ldots,N\} with weights λ 1 ​ ( i ) , … , λ N ​ ( i ) \lambda_{1}(i),\ldots,\lambda_{N}(i) . The mixture weights are then set proportionally to these same scores, restricted to the selected slots, ω i , c = λ c ​ ( i ) ∑ l ∈ 𝒞 ⁡ ( i ) λ l ​ ( i ) , \omega_{i,c}=\frac{\lambda_{c}(i)}{\sum_{l\in\mathcal{C}(i)}\lambda_{l}(i)}, (54) so that conditioning states closer to x t i x_{t}^{i} contribute more strongly to its own proposal.

sections.heading: Rao-Blackwellized mixture sampling.
sections.text: We now explain how expectations under m 0 | t θ ( ⋅ | x t i ) m^{\theta}_{0|t}(\cdot|x_{t}^{i}) are computed. Just as in NF 2 M-IS, we draw one base batch of M M i.i.d. candidates ξ j , 1 , 1 , … , ξ j , 1 , M ∼ q 0 | t θ ( ⋅ | x t j ) \xi_{j,1,1},\ldots,\xi_{j,1,M}\sim q^{\theta}_{0|t}(\cdot|x_{t}^{j}) for every trajectory j = 1 , … , N j=1,\ldots,N (this is the batches drawn under each source j j in Fig. 3 ). To assemble trajectory i i ’s C ​ M CM candidates, each slot c ∈ 𝒞 ⁡ ( i ) c\in\mathcal{C}(i) draws on the batch of its conditioning trajectory: the first time a trajectory is used as a component it reuses the shared base batch, as source j = 2 j=2 does for both receiving trajectories in the figure. Because 𝒞 ⁡ ( i ) \mathcal{C}(i) is a multiset, however, the same trajectory can occupy more than one slot of the same mixture; reusing one batch twice within a single mixture would break the independence the estimator below relies on, so each repeated occurrence instead draws a fresh, independent batch. Writing r ⁡ ( i , c ) r(i,c) for the occurrence number of slot c c within 𝒞 ⁡ ( i ) \mathcal{C}(i) (its first, second, … appearance), we denote the resulting candidates x 0 i , c , m = ξ c , r ⁡ ( i , c ) , m , ξ j , r , m ∼ q 0 | t θ ( ⋅ ∣ x t j ) , m = 1 , … , M , \displaystyle x_{0}^{i,c,m}=\xi_{c,\,r(i,c),\,m},\qquad\xi_{j,r,m}\sim q^{\theta}_{0|t}(\cdot\mid x_{t}^{j}),\quad m=1,\ldots,M, where batches are shared across every trajectory whose component set calls for the same pair ( j , r ) (j,r) , and drawn independently otherwise. This lets us reuse our expensive flow samples as much as possible while still having independent candidates within each trajectory’s own mixture. Expectations under m 0 | t θ ( ⋅ | x t i ) m^{\theta}_{0|t}(\cdot|x_{t}^{i}) can then be computed in a Rao-Blackwellized fashion, by conditioning on the mixture component rather than sampling it: 𝔼 m θ 0 | t ( ⋅ ∣ x t i ) [ ϕ ( X 0 i ) ] = ∑ c ∈ 𝒞 ⁡ ( i ) ω i , c 𝔼 q θ 0 | t ( ⋅ ∣ x t c ) [ ϕ ( X 0 i , c ) ] ≈ 1 M ∑ c ∈ 𝒞 ⁡ ( i ) ∑ m = 1 M ω i , c ϕ ( x 0 i , c , m ) . \mathbb{E}_{m^{\theta}_{0|t}(\cdot\mid x_{t}^{i})}\left[\phi(X^{i}_{0})\right]=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}(i)}\omega_{i,c}\,\mathbb{E}_{q^{\theta}_{0|t}(\cdot\mid x_{t}^{c})}\left[\phi(X_{0}^{i,c})\right]\approx\frac{1}{M}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}(i)}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\omega_{i,c}\,\phi\!\left(x_{0}^{i,c,m}\right). (55)

sections.heading: Self-normalized importance sampling for the reverse kernel.
sections.text: We now return to the denoising kernel approximation. Writing the exact transition as an expectation under the mixture proposal, p s | t ​ ( x s i ∣ x t i ) \displaystyle p_{s|t}(x^{i}_{s}\mid x^{i}_{t}) = ∫ p s | t , 0 ​ ( x s i ∣ x t i , x 0 i ) ​ p 0 | t ​ ( x 0 i ∣ x t i ) ​ d ​ x 0 i \displaystyle=\int p_{s|t,0}(x^{i}_{s}\mid x^{i}_{t},x^{i}_{0})\,p_{0|t}(x^{i}_{0}\mid x^{i}_{t})\,\mathrm{d}x^{i}_{0} = ∫ p s | t , 0 ​ ( x s i ∣ x t i , x 0 i ) ​ p 0 | t ​ ( x 0 i ∣ x t i ) m 0 | t θ ​ ( x 0 i ∣ x t i ) ​ m 0 | t θ ​ ( x 0 i ∣ x t i ) ​ d ​ x 0 i \displaystyle=\int p_{s|t,0}(x^{i}_{s}\mid x^{i}_{t},x^{i}_{0})\,\frac{p_{0|t}(x^{i}_{0}\mid x^{i}_{t})}{m^{\theta}_{0|t}(x^{i}_{0}\mid x^{i}_{t})}\,m^{\theta}_{0|t}(x^{i}_{0}\mid x^{i}_{t})\,\mathrm{d}x^{i}_{0} = 𝔼 m θ 0 | t ( ⋅ ∣ x t i ) [ p 0 | t ​ ( X 0 i ∣ x t i ) m 0 | t θ ​ ( X 0 i ∣ x t i ) p s | t , 0 ( x s i ∣ x t i , X 0 i ) ] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{m^{\theta}_{0|t}(\cdot\mid x_{t}^{i})}\!\left[\frac{p_{0|t}(X_{0}^{i}\mid x_{t}^{i})}{m^{\theta}_{0|t}(X_{0}^{i}\mid x_{t}^{i})}\,p_{s|t,0}(x^{i}_{s}\mid x^{i}_{t},X_{0}^{i})\right] ≈ ∑ c ∈ 𝒞 ⁡ ( i ) ∑ m = 1 M ω i , c ​ Λ i , c , m ​ p s | t , 0 ​ ( x s i ∣ x t i , x 0 i , c , m ) , \displaystyle\approx\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}(i)}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\omega_{i,c}\,\Lambda_{i,c,m}\,p_{s|t,0}(x^{i}_{s}\mid x^{i}_{t},x_{0}^{i,c,m}), where the last line applies the Rao-Blackwellized estimator ( 55 ), replacing the intractable ratio p 0 | t / m 0 | t θ p_{0|t}/m^{\theta}_{0|t} by a self-normalized importance weight Λ i , c , m \Lambda_{i,c,m} . Concretely, the unnormalized weights are Λ ~ i , c , m = p 0 | t ​ ( x 0 i , c , m ∣ x t i ) m 0 | t θ ​ ( x 0 i , c , m ∣ x t i ) ∝ p t | 0 ​ ( x t i ∣ x 0 i , c , m ) ​ exp ⁡ { − ℰ ⁡ ( x 0 i , c , m ) } ∑ c ′ ∈ 𝒞 ⁡ ( i ) ω i , c ′ ​ q 0 | t θ ​ ( x 0 i , c , m ∣ x t c ′ ) . \displaystyle\tilde{\Lambda}_{i,c,m}=\frac{p_{0|t}(x_{0}^{i,c,m}\mid x^{i}_{t})}{m^{\theta}_{0|t}(x_{0}^{i,c,m}\mid x^{i}_{t})}\propto\frac{p_{t|0}(x^{i}_{t}\mid x_{0}^{i,c,m})\,\exp\{-\mathcal{E}(x_{0}^{i,c,m})\}}{\sum_{c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}(i)}\omega_{i,c^{\prime}}\,q^{\theta}_{0|t}\left(x_{0}^{i,c,m}\mid x_{t}^{c^{\prime}}\right)}. Because these weights only enter the final mixture in combination with ω i , c \omega_{i,c} , we normalize the two together in one step, Ω i , c , m = ω i , c ​ Λ ~ i , c , m ∑ c ′ ∈ 𝒞 ⁡ ( i ) ∑ m ′ = 1 M ω i , c ′ ​ Λ ~ i , c ′ , m ′ . \Omega_{i,c,m}=\frac{\omega_{i,c}\,\tilde{\Lambda}_{i,c,m}}{\sum_{c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}(i)}\sum_{m^{\prime}=1}^{M}\omega_{i,c^{\prime}}\,\tilde{\Lambda}_{i,c^{\prime},m^{\prime}}}. (56) This gives a new mixture approximation of p s | t p_{s|t} , p ^ s | t 𝒞 , M , θ ​ ( x s i ∣ x t i ) = ∑ c ∈ 𝒞 ⁡ ( i ) ∑ m = 1 M Ω i , c , m ​ p s | t , 0 ​ ( x s i ∣ x t i , x 0 i , c , m ) , \hat{p}^{\mathcal{C},M,\theta}_{s|t}(x^{i}_{s}\mid x^{i}_{t})=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}(i)}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\Omega_{i,c,m}\;p_{s|t,0}(x^{i}_{s}\mid x^{i}_{t},x_{0}^{i,c,m}), (57) composed at the cost of only M M flow draws per component, yet at least as expressive than the M M -candidate proposal of NF 2 M-IS.

sections.heading: The computational catch and the autoregressive blessing.
sections.text: This added expressiveness is not free: computing Ω i , c , m \Omega_{i,c,m} requires the cross-likelihoods q 0 | t θ ​ ( x 0 i , c , m ∣ x t c ′ ) , for all ​ c , c ′ ∈ 𝒞 ⁡ ( i ) . \displaystyle q^{\theta}_{0|t}\left(x_{0}^{i,c,m}\mid x_{t}^{c^{\prime}}\right),\qquad\text{for all }c,c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}(i). The C C "diagonal" terms q 0 | t θ ​ ( x 0 i , c ¯ , m | x t c ¯ ) q^{\theta}_{0|t}(x_{0}^{i,\bar{c},m}|x_{t}^{\bar{c}}) are returned for free with each flow sample and, like the samples themselves, are reused whenever a slot shares its source ( Fig. 3 ). Only the remaining C ⁡ ( C − 1 ) C(C-1) cross terms per trajectory need a new evaluation, giving at most N ​ M ​ C ​ ( C − 1 ) NMC(C-1) additional evaluations per level (zero when C = 1 C=1 , where the mixture collapses to NF 2 M-IS) and less in practice when component sets overlap across trajectories. This overhead stays comparatively harmless for an autoregressive flow, where sampling is sequential and linear in token count but density evaluation is a single parallel pass: since sampling cost dominates, the batch-sharing scheme of Fig. 3 is what drives wall-clock cost, while the extra cross-likelihoods remain comparatively negligible. The full sampler is summarized in Alg. 3 . sections.heading: Amortized cost.
sections.text: Let U U denote the number of distinct pairs ( j , r ) (j,r) drawn across the ensemble at a given level. Candidate generation then costs U ​ M UM flow samples, with N ≤ U ≤ N ​ C N\leq U\leq NC , against N ​ C ​ M NCM without sharing. The lower bound U = N U=N holds when no source repeats within any single trajectory’s 𝒞 ⁡ ( i ) \mathcal{C}(i) : every external pick then falls at its first occurrence, already drawn by its source for itself, so cross-trajectory sharing is automatic. Such repeats become rarer as the proximity weights λ j ​ ( i ) \lambda_{j}(i) spread across more indices, the high-noise regime of ( 17 ) ( β t → 0 \beta_{t}\to 0 ). The upper bound U = N ​ C U=NC is reached e.g. if every trajectory fills all C C slots with itself: no batch is ever shared, and the mixture collapses to a single density, paying C × C\times the sampling cost of NF 2 M-IS for none of its added expressiveness.

sections.heading: Empirical ablation
sections.text: Figure 4: Average effective sample size of q 0 | t θ ( ⋅ | x t ) q^{\theta}_{0|t}(\cdot|x_{t}) against p 0 | t ( ⋅ | x t ) p_{0|t}(\cdot|x_{t}) as a function of t t , for NF 2 M-IS and NF 2 M-MIS across different numbers of importance candidates or mixture components. M ⋆ M^{\star} denotes the budget reported in Tab. 18 . Figure 5: Inference time and distributional distances for all systems, comparing NF 2 M-IS and NF 2 M-MIS across different numbers of importance candidates or mixture components. M ⋆ M^{\star} denotes the budget reported in Tab. 18 . We compare the performance of NF 2 M-MIS against NF 2 M-IS along two axes: candidate-pool quality and downstream performance. Fig. 4 reports the average effective sample size at each denoising transition, and shows that NF 2 M-MIS with C C components and M M candidates per component matches the pool quality of NF 2 M-IS run with C ​ M CM independent candidates, confirming that sharing candidates across trajectories does not degrade the proposal. However, both methods exhibit low inner ESS, particularly for chignolin and at the lowest noise levels, indicating substantial importance-weight concentration. This is surprising, as noise levels near t = 0 t=0 should make the target easiest to approximate. We hypothesize instead that the near-deterministic posterior forces the flow’s affine-coupling scale network into a high-variance regime that is difficult to learn. Preconditioning the flow with techniques akin to Karras et al. (2022) often degraded performance rather than fixing this. Fortunately, this is precisely the regime where the MAExL steps ( Sec. A.3 ) are most accurate, compensating for the weak proposal. Fig. 5 shows that this parity carries over to downstream distributional distances, with the two methods performing on par at matched budgets. The left panel of Fig. 5 shows that inference time is likewise comparable between the two methods. This can be explained at our current scale, since for molecules this small the autoregressive flow’s sampling and log-likelihood costs are already comparable on a modern GPU, leaving little headroom for the sharing scheme in NF 2 M-MIS to reduce wall-clock time. We expect this gap to widen in NF 2 M-MIS’s favor as system size grows and sampling cost increasingly dominates evaluation cost. Finally, Fig. 5 confirms the expected trend that both methods’ metrics improve monotonically as the candidate budget increases.

sections.heading: A.3 Metropolis-Adjusted Exponential Langevin
sections.text: A recurring subroutine in our pipeline is sampling from a posterior whose likelihood is an isotropic Gaussian in the latent variable. This subsection describes the kernel we use for that subroutine: a Metropolis-adjusted exponential integrator of the corresponding Langevin diffusion, designed to remain stable across the full range of likelihood scales encountered during inference.

sections.heading: Connection to score-matching trade-offs.
sections.text: The two ends of the τ \tau -range, global likelihood-scale moves and local MALA moves on the posterior score, mirror the tension between using the likelihood (Tweedie’s identity, denoising-score-matching style) and the posterior score (target-score-matching style) as the primary signal; a growing line of work argues that neither extreme is universally best Bortoli et al. (2024) ; Kahouli et al. (2025) ; Young et al. (2026) ; Blessing et al. (2026) . Our step-size adaptation lets the sampler choose its own balance, per chain and per noise level.

The effect is concentrated almost entirely in the energy metric. Disabling MAExL degrades ℰ \mathcal{E} - 𝒲 2 \mathcal{W}_{2} on every system and for both weighting schemes, in most cases by a factor of two or more, and on ALA-4 it is what separates a usable estimator from an unreliable one: without MAExL the energy discrepancy grows by an order of magnitude and its across-seed standard deviation exceeds its mean, i.e. individual seeds fail outright, while the same configuration with MAExL steps is both accurate and tightly concentrated. MAExL therefore buys run-to-run reproducibility as much as average accuracy. By contrast, 𝕋 \mathbb{T} - 𝒲 2 \mathcal{W}_{2} is essentially flat across the three settings on all five systems, moving by at most a few percent and generally within one seed standard deviation. This is what one expects from a local, p 0 | t p_{0|t} -invariant kernel: MAExL relaxes energetic strain in the proposed x 0 x_{0} configurations, the clashes and distorted bonds that dominate the energy distribution, but its moves are too local to transfer probability mass between torsional metastable states, so the dihedral marginals remain governed by the coverage of the learned model. The price is modest and shrinks in relative terms with system size, since on the larger systems the flow evaluations and the post-hoc MALA ladder dominate the inference budget. Returns also saturate well before the largest setting: 512 and 1024 steps are statistically indistinguishable for NF 2 M-IS and nominally favour the shorter chains on the three largest systems, with only NF 2 M-MIS showing a consistent preference for 1024 steps.

sections.heading: A.4 Centre-of-mass adjustment for the conditional posterior
sections.text: We follow the Gaussian centre-of-mass (CoM) augmentation of SBG ( Tan et al., 2025 ) and extend it to our diffusion posterior. Unlike SBG, we do not use a radial correction: every weight below is built from the Cartesian density of the centroid. We first derive valid importance weights and then, separately, characterise when matching the centroid proposal improves the effective sample size (ESS).

sections.heading: A.4.1 Setup and notation
sections.text: For x = ( x 1 , … , x N ) ∈ ℝ N ​ d x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N})\in\mathbb{R}^{Nd} , let c = N − 1 ​ ∑ i x i c=N^{-1}\sum_{i}x_{i} be the unweighted centroid, which is what we mean by the CoM throughout, and let x ^ = x − 𝟏 N ⊗ c \hat{x}=x-\mathbf{1}_{N}\otimes c be the centred configuration. Then x = x ^ + 𝟏 N ⊗ c , x ^ ∈ ℋ := { s ∈ ℝ N ​ d : ∑ i s i = 0 } . \displaystyle x=\hat{x}+\mathbf{1}_{N}\otimes c,\qquad\hat{x}\in\mathcal{H}:=\Bigl\{s\in\mathbb{R}^{Nd}:\textstyle\sum_{i}s_{i}=0\Bigr\}. The two components are orthogonal, and dim ℋ = ( N − 1 ) ​ d \dim\mathcal{H}=(N-1)d . All densities below are written in the coordinates ( x ^ , c ) (\hat{x},c) , with respect to Lebesgue measure on ℋ × ℝ d \mathcal{H}\times\mathbb{R}^{d} . The change of variables to Cartesian coordinates has a constant Jacobian, which we include whenever the flow density is expressed in these coordinates. Let p p be the normalised Boltzmann density on ℋ \mathcal{H} . Restricting to ℋ \mathcal{H} removes the translational degree of freedom, which would otherwise make the density unnormalisable. As in SBG, we lift p p to the ambient space by attaching an independent Gaussian centroid: p ~ ​ ( x ^ , c ) = p ⁡ ( x ^ ) ​ g σ ​ ( c ) , g σ ​ ( c ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( c , 0 , σ 2 ​ I d ) , σ 2 = 1 / N . \tilde{p}(\hat{x},c)=p(\hat{x})\,g_{\sigma}(c),\qquad g_{\sigma}(c)=\mathcal{N}(c;0,\sigma^{2}I_{d}),\qquad\sigma^{2}=1/N. (71) This variance is that of the centroid of N N independent standard Gaussian vectors. Since g σ g_{\sigma} integrates to one, the centred marginal of p ~ \tilde{p} is exactly p p .

sections.heading: A.4.2 Relation to SBG’s unconditional adjustment
sections.text: Like SBG, we introduce an auxiliary Gaussian centroid so that the model can be trained in the full ambient space; we differ in the density used for reweighting. For d = 3 d=3 , the radius r = ‖ c ‖ r=\|c\| has density f σ ​ ( r ) = 1 σ ​ χ 3 ​ ( r / σ ) = 4 ​ π ​ r 2 ​ g σ ​ ( c ) , ‖ c ‖ = r , \displaystyle f_{\sigma}(r)=\frac{1}{\sigma}\chi_{3}(r/\sigma)=4\pi r^{2}g_{\sigma}(c),\qquad\|c\|=r, where the factor 4 ​ π ​ r 2 4\pi r^{2} arises from integrating the spherical volume element over the angles. Thus f σ f_{\sigma} is a density with respect to d ​ r dr , whereas g σ g_{\sigma} is a density with respect to d ​ c dc . SBG’s Eq. (5) subtracts log ⁡ f σ ​ ( ‖ c ‖ ) \log f_{\sigma}(\|c\|) from the flow log-density. For the Gaussian lift ( 71 ), however, the correct unconditional importance weight is w ⁡ ( x ) ∝ p ⁡ ( x ^ ) ​ g σ ​ ( c ) q θ ​ ( x ) . \displaystyle w(x)\propto\frac{p(\hat{x})\,g_{\sigma}(c)}{q^{\theta}(x)}. Rewriting the denominator as q θ / g σ q^{\theta}/g_{\sigma} amounts to adding ‖ c ‖ 2 / ( 2 ​ σ 2 ) \|c\|^{2}/(2\sigma^{2}) to the flow log-density, up to an additive constant. We omit SBG’s additional − 2 ​ log ⁡ ‖ c ‖ -2\log\|c\| term, since it stems from the radial Jacobian rather than from the Cartesian Gaussian density.

sections.heading: A.4.3 The conditional Gaussian lift
sections.text: We consider variance-exploding noising with α t = 1 \alpha_{t}=1 and σ t > 0 \sigma_{t}>0 : X t | X 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( X 0 , σ t 2 ​ I N ​ d ) . \displaystyle X_{t}\mid X_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(X_{0},\sigma_{t}^{2}I_{Nd}). The conditional flow q 0 | t θ q^{\theta}_{0|t} is trained on pairs ( x 0 , x t ) (x_{0},x_{t}) generated by first augmenting with a Gaussian centroid and then applying this noising. The posterior over centred configurations is p 0 | t ⟂ ​ ( x ^ 0 ∣ x ^ t ) ∝ p ⁡ ( x ^ 0 ) ​ exp ⁡ ( − ‖ x ^ t − x ^ 0 ‖ 2 2 ​ σ t 2 ) , p^{\perp}_{0|t}(\hat{x}_{0}\mid\hat{x}_{t})\propto p(\hat{x}_{0})\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|\hat{x}_{t}-\hat{x}_{0}\|^{2}}{2\sigma_{t}^{2}}\right), (72) whereas the lifted model has posterior p ~ 0 | t ​ ( x 0 ∣ x t ) ∝ 𝒩 ⁡ ( x t , x 0 , σ t 2 ​ I N ​ d ) ​ p ​ ( x ^ 0 ) ​ g σ ​ ( c 0 ) . \tilde{p}_{0|t}(x_{0}\mid x_{t})\propto\mathcal{N}(x_{t};x_{0},\sigma_{t}^{2}I_{Nd})\,p(\hat{x}_{0})\,g_{\sigma}(c_{0}). (73) Here and below, evaluating a density at x 0 x_{0} is shorthand for evaluating it at ( x ^ 0 , c 0 ) (\hat{x}_{0},c_{0}) in the coordinates fixed above. The squared distance splits orthogonally as ‖ x t − x 0 ‖ 2 = ‖ x ^ t − x ^ 0 ‖ 2 + N ​ ‖ c t − c 0 ‖ 2 , \displaystyle\|x_{t}-x_{0}\|^{2}=\|\hat{x}_{t}-\hat{x}_{0}\|^{2}+N\|c_{t}-c_{0}\|^{2}, so the centroid is observed through the Gaussian likelihood c t | c 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( c 0 , σ t 2 ​ I d / N ) . \displaystyle c_{t}\mid c_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(c_{0},\sigma_{t}^{2}I_{d}/N). Combining this likelihood with the Gaussian prior g σ g_{\sigma} yields the factorisation p ~ 0 | t ​ ( x 0 ∣ x t ) = p 0 | t ⟂ ​ ( x ^ 0 ∣ x ^ t ) ​ g t ​ ( c 0 ∣ c t ) , g t ​ ( c 0 ∣ c t ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( c 0 , η t ​ c t , β t 2 ​ I d ) , \tilde{p}_{0|t}(x_{0}\mid x_{t})=p^{\perp}_{0|t}(\hat{x}_{0}\mid\hat{x}_{t})\,g_{t}(c_{0}\mid c_{t}),\qquad g_{t}(c_{0}\mid c_{t})=\mathcal{N}(c_{0};\eta_{t}c_{t},\beta_{t}^{2}I_{d}), (74) where η t \displaystyle\eta_{t} = σ 2 σ 2 + σ t 2 / N = 1 1 + σ t 2 , \displaystyle=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\sigma^{2}+\sigma_{t}^{2}/N}=\frac{1}{1+\sigma_{t}^{2}}, (75) β t 2 \displaystyle\beta_{t}^{2} = σ 2 ​ ( σ t 2 / N ) σ 2 + σ t 2 / N = σ t 2 N ⁡ ( 1 + σ t 2 ) , \displaystyle=\frac{\sigma^{2}(\sigma_{t}^{2}/N)}{\sigma^{2}+\sigma_{t}^{2}/N}=\frac{\sigma_{t}^{2}}{N(1+\sigma_{t}^{2})}, and the second equalities use σ 2 = 1 / N \sigma^{2}=1/N . In particular, lifting before conditioning leaves the centred posterior ( 72 ) unchanged.

sections.heading: Rotations.
sections.text: If p p is rotationally invariant, the lifted posterior is jointly rotation invariant: for every R ∈ SO ⁡ ( d ) R\in\mathrm{SO}(d) , acting identically on each particle, p ~ 0 | t ​ ( R ​ x 0 ∣ R ​ x t ) = p ~ 0 | t ​ ( x 0 ∣ x t ) . \tilde{p}_{0|t}(Rx_{0}\mid Rx_{t})=\tilde{p}_{0|t}(x_{0}\mid x_{t}). (76) This is invariance under rotating x 0 x_{0} and x t x_{t} together, not under rotating x 0 x_{0} alone at fixed x t x_{t} . Neither the factorisation above nor the weights below require rotational invariance; both follow solely from the independent Gaussian lift and the orthogonal split of the likelihood.

sections.heading: A.4.4 Importance weights and effective log-likelihood
sections.text: Fix t t and x t x_{t} , and draw independent samples from the learned flow q 0 | t θ ( ⋅ | x t ) q^{\theta}_{0|t}(\cdot\,|\,x_{t}) , whose support we assume covers that of the lifted posterior. The importance weights are w t ​ ( x 0 ) = p 0 | t ⟂ ​ ( x ^ 0 ∣ x ^ t ) ​ g t ​ ( c 0 ∣ c t ) q 0 | t θ ​ ( x 0 ∣ x t ) , w_{t}(x_{0})=\frac{p^{\perp}_{0|t}(\hat{x}_{0}\mid\hat{x}_{t})\,g_{t}(c_{0}\mid c_{t})}{q^{\theta}_{0|t}(x_{0}\mid x_{t})}, (77) where normalising constants independent of x 0 x_{0} may be dropped in practice. These weights do not require the learned flow to factorise. Indeed, since g t ( ⋅ | c t ) g_{t}(\cdot\,|\,c_{t}) integrates to one, every integrable centred observable F F satisfies 𝔼 q 0 | t θ ​ [ w t ​ ( X 0 ) ​ F ​ ( X ^ 0 ) ] = ∫ ℋ F ⁡ ( s ) ​ p 0 | t ⟂ ​ ( s ∣ x ^ t ) ​ 𝑑 s . \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{q^{\theta}_{0|t}}\bigl[w_{t}(X_{0})\,F(\hat{X}_{0})\bigr]=\int_{\mathcal{H}}F(s)\,p^{\perp}_{0|t}(s\mid\hat{x}_{t})\,ds. Taking F ≡ 1 F\equiv 1 gives 𝔼 q 0 | t θ ​ [ w t ] = 1 \mathbb{E}_{q^{\theta}_{0|t}}[w_{t}]=1 , so self-normalised importance sampling is consistent for such observables. To compare with SBG’s log-likelihood adjustment, we define the effective log-likelihood log ⁡ q 0 | t θ , eff ​ ( x 0 ∣ x t ) \displaystyle\log q^{\theta,\mathrm{eff}}_{0|t}(x_{0}\mid x_{t}) : = log ⁡ q 0 | t θ ​ ( x 0 ∣ x t ) − log ⁡ g t ​ ( c 0 ∣ c t ) \displaystyle:=\log q^{\theta}_{0|t}(x_{0}\mid x_{t})-\log g_{t}(c_{0}\mid c_{t}) (78) = log q θ 0 | t ( x 0 ∣ x t ) + ‖ δ ‖ 2 2 ​ β t 2 + d 2 log ⁡ ( 2 ​ π ​ β t 2 ) , δ = c 0 − η t c t , \displaystyle=\log q^{\theta}_{0|t}(x_{0}\mid x_{t})+\frac{\|\delta\|^{2}}{2\beta_{t}^{2}}+\frac{d}{2}\log(2\pi\beta_t^2),\qquad\delta=c_{0}-\eta_{t}c_{t}, so that w t = p 0 | t ⟂ / q 0 | t θ , eff w_{t}=p^{\perp}_{0|t}/q^{\theta,\mathrm{eff}}_{0|t} . This merely rewrites ( 77 ); it is not a new sampling proposal. In general, q 0 | t θ , eff q^{\theta,\mathrm{eff}}_{0|t} is neither normalised on the ambient space nor equal to the centred marginal of the flow. Note that the first factor in the numerator of ( 77 ) is the centred posterior ( 72 ), not the lifted posterior ( 73 ). Equivalently, the entire numerator may be replaced by the lifted posterior, that is, the full likelihood times p ⁡ ( x ^ 0 ) ​ g σ ​ ( c 0 ) p(\hat{x}_{0})\,g_{\sigma}(c_{0}) , which already contains the centroid factor. Either way, the Gaussian centroid factor must not be included twice.

sections.text: For K K independent proposal samples with weights w 1 , … , w K w_{1},\ldots,w_{K} , the effective sample size is ESS K = ( ∑ i = 1 K w i ) 2 ∑ i = 1 K w i 2 . \displaystyle\mathrm{ESS}_{K}=\frac{\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{K}w_{i}\bigr)^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{K}w_{i}^{2}}. For a normalised target π \pi and a proposal q q whose support covers that of π \pi , if w = π / q w=\pi/q has a finite second moment, then ESS K K → K → ∞ a . s . ρ ⁡ ( q , π ) := ( 𝔼 q ​ [ w ] ) 2 𝔼 q ​ [ w 2 ] . \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{ESS}_{K}}{K}\xrightarrow[K\to\infty]{\mathrm{a.s.}}\rho(q,\pi):=\frac{(\mathbb{E}_{q}[w])^{2}}{\mathbb{E}_{q}[w^{2}]}. Our comparison concerns this asymptotic fractional ESS, not the ESS of any particular finite sample. Proposition 20 (Matching the centroid proposal) Fix t t and x t x_{t} , and write P ⁡ ( s ) = p 0 | t ⟂ ​ ( s | x ^ t ) P(s)=p^{\perp}_{0|t}(s\,|\,\hat{x}_{t}) and g ⁡ ( c ) = g t ​ ( c | c t ) g(c)=g_{t}(c\,|\,c_{t}) . Consider the lifted target π ⁡ ( s , c ) = P ⁡ ( s ) ​ g ​ ( c ) \pi(s,c)=P(s)\,g(c) and the two proposals q ⁡ ( s , c ) = Q ⁡ ( s ) ​ k ​ ( c ) , q match ​ ( s , c ) = Q ⁡ ( s ) ​ g ​ ( c ) . \displaystyle q(s,c)=Q(s)\,k(c),\qquad q_{\mathrm{match}}(s,c)=Q(s)\,g(c). Assume that all densities are normalised, that Q > 0 Q>0 wherever P > 0 P>0 and k > 0 k>0 wherever g > 0 g>0 (up to null sets), and that 𝔼 Q ​ [ ( P / Q ) 2 ] < ∞ , 𝔼 k ​ [ ( g / k ) 2 ] < ∞ . \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{Q}\bigl[(P/Q)^{2}\bigr]<\infty,\qquad\mathbb{E}_{k}\bigl[(g/k)^{2}\bigr]<\infty. Then ρ ⁡ ( q , π ) ≤ ρ ⁡ ( q match , π ) , \rho(q,\pi)\leq\rho(q_{\mathrm{match}},\pi), (79) with equality if and only if k = g k=g almost everywhere. Proof. Under q q , the weight factorises as w = A ⁡ ( S ) ​ B ​ ( C ) w=A(S)\,B(C) with A = P / Q A=P/Q and B = g / k B=g/k . These factors are independent and each has expectation one, so ρ ⁡ ( q , π ) = 1 𝔼 Q ​ [ A 2 ] ​ 𝔼 k ​ [ B 2 ] ≤ 1 𝔼 Q ​ [ A 2 ] = ρ ⁡ ( q match , π ) , \displaystyle\rho(q,\pi)=\frac{1}{\mathbb{E}_{Q}[A^{2}]\,\mathbb{E}_{k}[B^{2}]}\leq\frac{1}{\mathbb{E}_{Q}[A^{2}]}=\rho(q_{\mathrm{match}},\pi), where the inequality follows from 𝔼 k ​ [ B 2 ] ≥ ( 𝔼 k ​ B ) 2 = 1 \mathbb{E}_{k}[B^{2}]\geq(\mathbb{E}_{k}B)^{2}=1 . Equality holds exactly when B = 1 B=1 k k -almost surely, that is, when k = g k=g almost everywhere. ∎ The proof relies on the same independent-weight factorisation as SBG ( Tan et al., 2025 , Appendix B.1) . It differs from their Proposition 1 in that it compares two normalised proposals against a single fixed, normalised target, under explicit moment assumptions. It is therefore a statement about proposal matching and provides no additional ESS guarantee for the effective log-likelihood. Several consequences follow. If the flow already factorises as q 0 | t θ = Q ​ g t q^{\theta}_{0|t}=Q\,g_{t} , its ordinary lifted-target weights reduce to P / Q P/Q , because the centroid factor cancels; if moreover Q = P Q=P , all weights are constant. sections.heading: Limits.
sections.text: For fixed x t x_{t} , as σ t → ∞ \sigma_{t}\to\infty we have η t → 0 \eta_{t}\to 0 and β t 2 → σ 2 \beta_{t}^{2}\to\sigma^{2} , which recovers the unconditional Gaussian adjustment above rather than SBG’s radial formula. As σ t → 0 \sigma_{t}\to 0 , we have η t → 1 \eta_{t}\to 1 and β t 2 → 0 \beta_{t}^{2}\to 0 , so the centroid posterior concentrates at c t c_{t} . At zero noise it becomes singular, which is why the density formulas are stated only for σ t > 0 \sigma_{t}>0 . Under g t g_{t} , writing δ = β t ​ Z \delta=\beta_{t}Z with Z ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I d ) Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) gives − log ⁡ g t ​ ( c 0 ∣ c t ) = ‖ Z ‖ 2 2 + d 2 ​ log ⁡ ( 2 ​ π ​ β t 2 ) . \displaystyle-\log g_{t}(c_{0}\mid c_{t})=\frac{\|Z\|^{2}}{2}+\frac{d}{2}\log(2\pi\beta_t^2). The second term is constant in x 0 x_{0} and cancels under self-normalisation, but the sample-dependent first term does not vanish at low noise. It does, however, cancel exactly in the importance ratio at every positive noise level whenever the proposal centroid matches g t g_{t} .

sections.heading: A.5 Conditional TarFlow and StarFlow
sections.text: Sec. 3.2 introduces our conditional molecular TarFlow and StarFlow backbones and the two mechanisms used to inject x t x_{t} . This appendix gives the detail that does not fit there: a brief recap of the two base architectures ( Sec. A.5.1 , pointing to their own papers for anything not needed below), exactly how time and space conditioning are added on top of them ( Sec. A.5.2 ), the cache that makes conditioning nearly free at sampling time ( Sec. A.5.3 ), and the resulting time and space complexity of every operation our sampler uses ( Sec. A.5.4 ).

sections.heading: TarFlow.
sections.text: TarFlow ( Zhai et al., 2025 ) is an autoregressive normalising flow built from causal-Transformer coupling layers. Given tokens x = ( x 1 , … , x N ) x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}) , x i ∈ ℝ D x_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} , one layer computes z i = ( x i − μ i ( x < i ) ) ⊙ exp ( − α i ( x < i ) ) , i = 1 , … , N , z_{i}=\bigl(x_{i}-\mu_{i}(x_{<i})\bigr)\odot\exp\bigl(-\alpha_{i}(x_{<i})\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,N, (80) with z 1 ≡ x 1 z_{1}\equiv x_{1} and ( μ i , α i ) (\mu_{i},\alpha_{i}) produced by a single causal-Transformer pass over the prefix x < i x_{<i} ; the Jacobian is lower-triangular, with log | det ∂ z / ∂ x | = − ∑ i 𝟏 ⊤ α i ( x < i ) \log|\det\partial z/\partial x|=-\sum_{i}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\alpha_{i}(x_{<i}) . Training computes every ( μ i , α i ) (\mu_{i},\alpha_{i}) in one parallel pass under a causal mask; sampling reruns the same Transformer autoregressively, with a standard KV cache. A deep flow stacks L L such layers, permuting the sequence between layers so every coordinate sits both early and late in the autoregressive order across the stack. We refer to Zhai et al. (2025) for the full architecture, including the image-patch tokenisation, which does not affect anything below.

sections.heading: StarFlow.
sections.text: StarFlow ( Gu et al., 2026 ) scales the same recipe with two changes we adopt. First, deep–shallow depth allocation : rather than L L equal layers, one deep block of ℓ \ell layers generates a first sample from noise and L − 1 L-1 shallow blocks of two layers each refine it, written ℓ ⁡ ( L ) \ell(L) - d d for width d d . Second, a guarded affine head : TarFlow’s exp ⁡ ( α i ) \exp(\alpha_i) overflows once | α i | ≈ 88 |\alpha_{i}|\approx 88 , so StarFlow soft-clips the pre-activation and passes it through a softplus instead, α ~ i = s ​ tanh ⁡ ( α i / s ) , σ i = softplus ⁡ ( α ~ i + softplus − 1 ​ ( 1 ) ) , z i = ( x i − μ i ) / σ i , \tilde{\alpha}_{i}=s\tanh(\alpha_i/s),\qquad\sigma_{i}=\mathrm{softplus}\bigl(\tilde{\alpha}_{i}+\mathrm{softplus}^{-1}(1)\bigr),\qquad z_{i}=(x_{i}-\mu_{i})/\sigma_{i}, (81) with s = 4 s=4 , which we use throughout, including for conditional TarFlow. StarFlow’s remaining two contributions (a pretrained-autoencoder latent space and a classifier-free guidance rule) are specific to text-to-image generation: an autoencoder would break the exactness of log ⁡ p θ \log p_{\theta} that our importance sampler needs, and there is no class or text label to guide on. We do not adopt either; see Gu et al. (2026) for both.

sections.heading: Molecular adaptation.
sections.text: Following Tan et al. (2025) , we tokenise an N N -atom configuration x ∈ ℝ N × 3 x\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 3} as one token per atom, so StarFlow’s 2-D patch grid becomes a degenerate 1 × N 1\times N image, and handle the target’s SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) symmetry outside the architecture through centering, a lifted centroid, and random rotation augmentation rather than through an equivariant backbone, Sec. 3.2 gives the details we share with the main text. Our molecular blocks use learned per-block positional embeddings rather than rotary ones, a choice Sec. A.5.3 returns to, full multi-head attention, GELU feed-forwards, and the guarded affine head of Eq. 81 . Per-system depth and width are given in Sec. B.2 .

sections.heading: A.5.2 Making the flow conditional on ( x t , t ) (x_{t},t)

Here y t y_{t} denotes the noisy configuration x t x_{t} of Sec. 3.2 , relabelled so the conditioning is never mistaken for another stage of the flow’s own x 0 , … , x T − 1 x^{0},\ldots,x^{T-1} sequence. The green/purple arrows are the inverse/forward instance of the same per-atom update between every pair of adjacent levels, x i ℓ = μ i ​ ( x < i ℓ ) + σ i ​ ( x < i ℓ ) ⋅ x i ℓ + 1 x^{\ell}_{i}=\mu_{i}(x^{\ell}_{<i})+\sigma_{i}(x^{\ell}_{<i})\cdot x^{\ell+1}_{i} (bottom left), x i ℓ + 1 x^{\ell+1}_{i} is literally z i z_{i} only at the very first level. y t y_{t} is shown entering as a causal prefix at the deep block only. Fig. 7 shows the cross-attention alternative and the every-block scope TarFlow uses instead ( Sec. Both directions read the same conditioning cache, built once from ( y t , t ) (y_{t},t) and shared across every particle drawn at that step ( Sec. A.5.3 ). Layout follows Gu et al. (2026) ’s own figure.

sections.heading: Time, via AdaLN-Zero.
sections.text: We follow DiT ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) : t t is embedded by a sinusoidal map and a two-layer MLP into a single vector c ∈ ℝ C c\in\mathbb{R}^{C} , which drives an AdaLN-Zero modulation in every attention layer of every block. A SiLU → Linear ⁡ ( C , 9 ​ C ) \mathrm{SiLU}\to\mathrm{Linear}(C,9C) produces a (shift, scale, gate) triple for each of the self-attention, cross-attention (when present) and MLP sub-layers, and every one of these modulation linears is zero-initialised. The unconditional flow already starts at the identity because its affine head is zero-initialised, while attention and the MLP still run live. The conditional flow starts at a strictly stronger identity, since every gate is zero too, so attention, cross-attention and the MLP contribute nothing at all, on top of the zero affine head.

sections.heading: Space, via cross-attention or a causal prefix.
sections.text: x t x_{t} enters through one of two mechanisms, both shown in Fig. 7 . Cross-attention projects x t x_{t} once per block through a shared ℝ 3 → ℝ C \mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{R}^{C} map, adds the same positional code used for the running x 0 x_{0} representation and lets each layer, every layer or a strided subset every m m -th one, project its own keys and values from that shared embedding and attend to it from a query built out of x 0 x_{0} . Prefix conditioning instead concatenates the projected, positionally-coded x t x_{t} ahead of x 0 x_{0} along the sequence axis and lets the block’s existing causal self-attention do the work: writing π \pi for the block’s permutation and W in , W cond W_{\mathrm{in}},W_{\mathrm{cond}} for the two input projections, z = [ W cond ​ x t π + p π + c ​ 𝟏 ⊤ ; W in ​ x 0 π + p π ] ∈ ℝ 2 ​ N × C , z=\bigl[\,W_{\mathrm{cond}}x_{t}^{\pi}+p^{\pi}+c\mathbf{1}^{\top}\,;\,W_{\mathrm{in}}x_{0}^{\pi}+p^{\pi}\,\bigr]\in\mathbb{R}^{2N\times C}, (82) reading ( μ i , α ~ i ) (\mu_{i},\tilde{\alpha}_{i}) off the last N N positions only. Because attention is causal and the prefix leads, the first N N positions never depend on x 0 x_{0} , so x 0 ↦ z x_{0}\mapsto z is still autoregressive with the same lower-triangular Jacobian. Every conditioning atom is simply visible to every query atom through the same attention operator that carries the autoregressive chain, at the cost of attending over 2 ​ N 2N rather than N N tokens and no parameters beyond W cond W_{\mathrm{cond}} . Both mechanisms are available to either backbone, but their scope differs. Conditional TarFlow conditions every block while conditional StarFlow restricts conditioning to the last (deep) block only, while every block still receives t t through its own AdaLN-Zero. In practice, cross-attention is what nearly every reported model uses: every TarFlow model, and StarFlow on every system but chignolin. Chignolin,the largest system with the deepest deep block, is the sole case where the prefix variant is selected instead, over its cross-attention twin at matched depth ( Tabs. 9 and 10 ). Figure 7: The two conditioning mechanisms, inside one block. (a) Cross-attention: x t x_{t} is embedded once per block, and each of the K K layers still projects its own keys and values from that shared embedding and attends to it from a query built out of x 0 x_{0} ; every sub-layer also carries an AdaLN-Zero modulation driven by the time embedding c c , with every modulation linear zero-initialised, so the block is the identity map at init. (b) Prefix: x t x_{t} instead joins the sequence as a causal prefix ( Eq. 82 ). A plain lower-triangular mask over the concatenated 2 ​ N 2N tokens already gives every target atom access to every conditioning atom while keeping the prefix invisible to x 0 x_{0} , so the added cost is a longer attention span and W cond W_{\mathrm{cond}} , not a new sub-layer. In both variants the conditioning state is fixed across every particle sharing x t x_{t} , hence cacheable ( Sec. A.5.3 ).

sections.heading: A.5.3 The conditioning cache
sections.text: x t x_{t} is fixed across every particle drawn from the same posterior: one denoising step of NF 2 M-IS/MIS scores and draws M M (or C ​ M CM ) particles against a single ( x t , t ) (x_{t},t) . Recomputing the conditioning pathway from scratch for each of them (the time embedding, the projected x t x_{t} tokens, and every conditioned layer’s cross-attention or prefix keys and values) would repeat identical work M M times over. Instead, a dedicated preparation step builds this state once per distinct ( x t , t ) (x_{t},t) , and every subsequent call to the flow takes it as an argument together with an index selecting each particle’s row, so only the row lookup runs per particle. We have verified this reduction bit-for-bit against recomputing the conditioning independently for every particle. For StarFlow under prefix conditioning this goes one step further: the object the preparation step builds is not a separate cache that later gets copied in, but literally the same key/value buffer the autoregressive sampling loop appends to, so pre-filling and decoding share one piece of memory rather than two.

sections.heading: A.5.4 Computational complexity
sections.text: We summarise the per-evaluation cost of the molecular TarFlow and StarFlow variants. Let N N be the number of atoms, C C the Transformer channel width and L L the number of blocks, with block ℓ \ell carrying K ℓ K_{\ell} attention layers, so that the full flow contains K tot = ∑ ℓ = 1 L K ℓ K_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}K_{\ell} layers. The TarFlow models set K ℓ = K K_{\ell}=K for every block, giving K tot = L ​ K K_{\mathrm{tot}}=LK and the StarFlow models set K ℓ = 2 K_{\ell}=2 for the shallow blocks and K ℓ = K deep K_{\ell}=K_{\mathrm{deep}} for the deep ones. We write K cond K_{\mathrm{cond}} for the number of layers that carry the x t x_{t} conditioning and m m for the cross-attention period, so that m = 1 m=1 places cross-attention on every layer. Tab. 5 gives the cost of a single call into the flow, Tab. 6 the cost once the conditioning cache of Sec. A.5.3 is in place. Every Transformer layer costs 𝒪 ⁡ ( N 2 ​ C + N ​ C 2 ) \mathcal{O}(N^{2}C+NC^{2}) : the attention matrix, plus the Q / K / V \mathrm{Q}/\mathrm{K}/\mathrm{V} and feed-forward linears. At the sizes we run, N N between 22 22 (alanine dipeptide) and 138 138 (chignolin), C C between 256 256 and 512 512 , the ratio of the two terms is C / N C/N , so the linear term dominates by an order of magnitude on the smallest system and still by roughly 4 × 4\times on the largest. The quadratic-in- N N attention cost is therefore not the binding constraint at this scale, and a forward pass is close to linear in the number of atoms.

sections.heading: Forward pass (density evaluation).
sections.text: All variants compute the entire collection { ( μ i , α i ) } i = 1 N \{(\mu_{i},\alpha_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} in a single parallel call with a causal attention mask, at a total cost of 𝒪 ⁡ ( K tot ​ ( N 2 ​ C + N ​ C 2 ) ) \mathcal{O}(K_{\mathrm{tot}}(N^{2}C+NC^{2})) . Cross-attention conditioning adds one further attention against x t x_{t} , also 𝒪 ⁡ ( N 2 ​ C + N ​ C 2 ) \mathcal{O}(N^{2}C+NC^{2}) , on every m m -th layer of the conditioned blocks, placing it on every layer ( m = 1 m=1 ) roughly doubles the per-layer constant, and larger m m scales that addition by 1 / m 1/m . Prefix conditioning instead runs the conditioned block over a sequence of length 2 ​ N 2N , costing 𝒪 ⁡ ( K cond ​ ( 4 ​ N 2 ​ C + 2 ​ N ​ C 2 ) ) \mathcal{O}(K_{\mathrm{cond}}(4N^{2}C+2NC^{2})) ; once the prefix keys and values have been pre-filled, only the N N target positions need to be projected and attended, which reduces this to 𝒪 ⁡ ( K cond ​ ( 2 ​ N 2 ​ C + N ​ C 2 ) ) \mathcal{O}(K_{\mathrm{cond}}(2N^{2}C+NC^{2})) . Neither form of conditioning changes the asymptotics, and prefix conditioning adds no parameters beyond the shared ℝ 3 → ℝ C \mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{R}^{C} projection.

sections.heading: Reverse pass (sampling).
sections.text: Sampling is inherently sequential along the autoregressive axis: producing token i + 1 i+1 requires the predictions ( μ i + 1 , α i + 1 ) (\mu_{i+1},\alpha_{i+1}) , which depend on the prefix z 1 : i + 1 z_{1:i+1} . With KV caching, each step extends the cached keys and values by one token and computes a query of length one against a prefix of length i + 1 i+1 , costing 𝒪 ⁡ ( ( i + 1 ) ​ C + C 2 ) \mathcal{O}((i{+}1)C+C^{2}) per attention layer. Summing over i = 0 , … , N − 1 i=0,\ldots,N{-}1 gives the same total 𝒪 ⁡ ( K tot ​ ( N 2 ​ C + N ​ C 2 ) ) \mathcal{O}(K_{\mathrm{tot}}(N^{2}C+NC^{2})) as the forward pass, but with a substantially larger constant due to the N N sequential kernel launches. Conditioning does not change that order, and neither mode lengthens the autoregressive chain: the conditioning is either attended in parallel with the decode step or pre-filled in a single parallel pass, so a draw is N N sequential steps whether or not the flow is conditioned. For cross-attention, the projection of x t x_{t} and its keys and values are computed once per block, outside the autoregressive loop, and reused for all N N steps; each step then costs 𝒪 ⁡ ( N ​ C + C 2 ) \mathcal{O}(NC+C^{2}) , contributing N 2 ​ C N^{2}C per conditioned layer against the N 2 ​ C / 2 N^{2}C/2 of the causal loop. For prefix conditioning, a single pre-fill of 𝒪 ⁡ ( K cond ​ ( N 2 ​ C + N ​ C 2 ) ) \mathcal{O}(K_{\mathrm{cond}}(N^{2}C+NC^{2})) populates the cache, after which step i i attends over N + i N+i keys rather than i i ; the sum is 3 ​ N 2 / 2 3N^{2}/2 against N 2 / 2 N^{2}/2 , i.e. three times the attention term of the bare causal loop, with the N ​ C 2 NC^{2} term unchanged. The real price is memory: the KV cache doubles in length, and its prefix half must be retained for as long as its conditioning row is alive. For the deep block of our chignolin model ( 20 20 layers, 138 138 conditioning tokens, 8 8 key/value heads of dimension 64 64 , in bfloat16) that is roughly 5.5 5.5 MiB per conditioning row, which is why the forward and reverse consumers read one shared store rather than each building its own ( Sec. A.5.3 ). The two conditioning modes therefore cost the same per decode step, K cond ​ N 2 ​ C K_{\mathrm{cond}}N^{2}C of extra attention, and differ only in what surrounds it: cross-attention pays for it in parameters, prefix conditioning pays for it in a pre-fill and a doubled cache, and the pre-fill is amortised over every particle that shares the conditioning row. Finally, the deep–shallow allocation reshapes where the sequential cost sits. Each of the L − 1 L-1 shallow blocks contributes only two layers, so the reverse pass is dominated by K deep K_{\mathrm{deep}} ; at a fixed K tot K_{\mathrm{tot}} the StarFlow allocation concentrates the sequential work in the same block that carries the conditioning, which is what makes the “condition the deep block only” choice of Sec. A.5.2 nearly free.
