sections.heading: Datasets.
sections.text: We reuse the molecular dynamics datasets of Tan et al. (2025) ; we briefly summarise them here for completeness and refer the reader to their Appendix D for full details. All datasets consist of all-atom Cartesian configurations sampled from MD trajectories generated with classical force fields in implicit solvent using OpenMM ( Eastman et al., 2017 ) . For each system, the first 1 ​ μ ​ s 1\mu s of trajectory is used for training, the next 0.2 ​ μ ​ s 0.2\mu s for validation, and the remainder for test, except for alanine dipeptide which follows the split of Klein and Noé (2024) . Some metastable states may be missing from the training set, which is the realistic regime in which we evaluate our models. The systems considered, in increasing order of size, are: • Alanine dipeptide (Amber ff99SBildn, 300 ​ K 300\mathrm{K} ): a single alanine residue capped by an acetyl group and an N-methyl group. We use the dataset and split of Klein and Noé (2024) , in which the lower-probability φ \varphi state is intentionally over-represented in training to provide a tractable but biased setting. • Trialanine (Amber 14, 310 ​ K 310\mathrm{K} ): three alanine residues without capping groups, generated as in Klein et al. (2023a) . • Alanine tetrapeptide (Amber ff99SBildn, 300 ​ K 300\mathrm{K} ): three alanines with acetyl and N-methyl caps. We use the system setup of Dibak et al. (2022) but treat all bonds as flexible (the original setup constrained hydrogen bonds for use with internal-coordinate flows). • Hexa-alanine (Amber 14, 310 ​ K 310\mathrm{K} ): six alanine residues without capping groups. • Chignolin (Amber 14, 310 ​ K 310\mathrm{K} ): the 10-residue protein GYDPETGTWG , 138 138 atoms, simulated for 4.5 ​ μ ​ s 4.5\mu s . Notable for forming a β \beta -hairpin in solvent ( Honda et al., 2004 ) . All MD simulations use a 1 ​ fs 1\mathrm{fs} integration time step. We use the same train/val/test trajectory splits, force fields, and evaluation subsets ( 10 4 10^{4} uniformly strided samples from the held-out portion) as Tan et al. (2025) to ensure direct comparability with their reported numbers.

sections.heading: Target energy evaluation.
sections.text: While the datasets themselves are generated by OpenMM MD, we do not call OpenMM to evaluate the target energy and its gradient at inference time: an OpenMM Context evaluates one configuration at a time with no batched interface, making it the dominant cost of importance-weighted and MCMC-refined evaluation. We instead reimplement the same potential (bonded, Lennard-Jones/Coulomb, and Generalized-Born terms, OBC1 or OBC2 depending on the system) as a batched PyTorch module whose parameters are read directly from the openmm.System , so OpenMM remains the sole authority on the force field, atom typing, and topology; only the summation, evaluated as vectorized tensor operations with exact autograd gradients in float32, is reimplemented. Validated against OpenMM’s double-precision Reference platform on 3.4 × 10 6 3.4\times 10^{6} configurations spanning all splits plus perturbed and clashing geometries, the worst-case deviation below 10 2 ​ k B ​ T 10^{2}\,k_{B}T is 1.2 × 10 − 5 ​ k B ​ T 1.2\times 10^{-5}\,k_{B}T in float64 and 7.7 × 10 − 4 ​ k B ​ T 7.7\times 10^{-4}\,k_{B}T in float32 (more accurate than OpenMM’s own CPU platform), whose internal single-precision nonbonded and GB evaluation deviates from the Reference platform by up to 3.3 × 10 − 4 ​ k B ​ T 3.3\times 10^{-4}\,k_{B}T on typical frames and 126 ​ k B ​ T 126\,k_{B}T near atomic clashes. This batched evaluation is 30 30 – 400 × 400\times faster per configuration than OpenMM’s serial loop and, unlike OpenMM’s hard failure on non-finite energies, returns a large but finite, differentiable energy at clashing configurations, avoiding sampler crashes during exploration.

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: For computational efficiency we subsample 10 4 10^{4} reference configurations from the held-out trajectory to serve as ground truth, and likewise restrict generated samples to a random subset of size 10 4 10^{4} when more are produced. We quantify distributional similarity using empirical Wasserstein-2 distances between generated and reference samples. Given two empirical distributions p = 1 n ​ ∑ i δ x i p=\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\delta_{x_{i}} and q = 1 m ​ ∑ j δ y j q=\tfrac{1}{m}\sum_{j}\delta_{y_{j}} , W 2 ​ ( p , q ) = min π ∈ Π ⁡ ( p , q ) ⁡ ∑ i , j π i ​ j ​ c ​ ( x i , y j ) 2 , \displaystyle W_{2}(p,q)=\min_{\pi\in\Pi(p,q)}\sqrt{\sum_{i,j}\pi_{ij}c(x_{i},y_{j})^{2}}, where the optimal coupling is computed with the POT library ( Flamary et al., 2021 ) . We use two cost functions: • Energy distance ( ℰ \mathcal{E} - 𝒲 2 \mathcal{W}_{2} ): the squared cost is c ℰ ​ ( x , y ) 2 = | E ⁡ ( x ) − E ⁡ ( y ) | 2 c_{\mathcal{E}}(x,y)^{2}=|E(x)-E(y)|^{2} where E E is the force-field potential energy. This metric is highly sensitive to fine-grained structural details (bond lengths, angles, clashes). • Dihedral torus distance ( 𝕋 \mathbb{T} - 𝒲 2 \mathcal{W}_{2} ): for a peptide with L L residues we extract the backbone dihedral angles Dihedrals ⁡ ( x ) = ( φ 1 , ψ 1 , … , φ L − 1 , ψ L − 1 ) \mathrm{Dihedrals}(x)=(\varphi_{1},\psi_{1},\ldots,\varphi_{L-1},\psi_{L-1}) , and use the wrapped squared cost on the torus c 𝕋 ​ ( x , y ) 2 = ∑ i = 1 2 ​ ( L − 1 ) [ ( Dihedrals ​ ( x ) i − Dihedrals ​ ( y ) i + π ) mod 2 ​ π − π ] 2 . \displaystyle c_{\mathbb{T}}(x,y)^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{2(L-1)}\big[(\mathrm{Dihedrals}(x)_{i}-\mathrm{Dihedrals}(y)_{i}+\pi)\bmod 2\pi-\pi\big]^{2}. This captures macrostructural information such as metastable-state occupancy and is robust to fine-grained noise.

sections.heading: B.2.1 Training
sections.text: The unconditional flows (TarFlow/StarFlow) and NF 2 M share one training recipe: AdamW ( β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.95 \beta_{2}=0.95 ) under bf16 mixed precision, gradient-norm clipping at 1.0 1.0 , and an EMA of the weights with decay 0.999 0.999 . Each model trains for 1000 epochs (195k steps) at batch size 512 over the 10 5 10^{5} training frames of the corresponding single-peptide system, on a single GPU, or with standard data-parallel DDP when more than one is used.

sections.heading: NF 2 M.
sections.text: NF 2 M trains with the loss of Sec. 3.2 , under an EDM noise schedule ( σ min = 10 − 3 \sigma_{\min}=10^{-3} , σ max = 40 \sigma_{\max}=40 ) ( Karras et al., 2022 ) and uniform weighting of the loss across noise levels. Every run uses the same optimizer recipe as the unconditional flows: learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , one-cycle schedule, weight decay 4 × 10 − 4 4\times 10^{-4} , 1000 epochs / 195k steps at batch 512. The conditional backbone is one of six variants, each defined relative to the corresponding unconditional preset (Tables 7 and 8 ): • T1 – a shallow TarFlow backbone, conditioned by cross-attention injected every 4th block; • K1 – the same shallow backbone as T1, but with cross-attention injected at every block; • W1 – the same shallow backbone as T1, widened rather than left narrow (channels + 64 +64 ); • S1 – a shallow-top-block StarFlow, conditioned through a single prefix token rather than cross-attention; • S1k – the same shallow-top-block StarFlow as S1, but conditioned by cross-attention rather than a prefix token; • S2 – StarFlow with no depth cut at all, conditioned by cross-attention. Cross-attention stride is min ⁡ ( 4 , l ) \min(4,l) , where l l is the variant’s (top-block) depth, so it falls back from every 4th block to every block on the shallowest variants. sections.heading: Velocity teacher.
sections.text: Before turning to the flow-map baselines (FALCON, FALCON-A, F2D2, SCALLOP), we describe the velocity field they all warm-start from and which we also evaluate as a standalone flow-matching baseline in the style of ECNF++ ( Tan et al., 2025 ) . A velocity field v ϕ v_{\phi} is trained by flow matching on the linear interpolant x t = ( 1 − t ) ​ x 0 + t ​ ε x_{t}=(1-t)\,x_{0}+t\,\varepsilon , with t ∈ [ 10 − 4 , 1 − 10 − 4 ] t\in[10^{-4},1-10^{-4}] : t = 0 t=0 is data and t = 1 t=1 is the prior. The network is the DiT backbone ( Ying et al., 2021 ; Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) of Tab. 11 . We use the antithetic variance reduction trick for the loss ( Albergo et al., 2025 ) . One teacher is trained per system, shared by all four flow-map methods and both of their pretraining objectives (below), and is always read at its EMA weights. Unlike every phase that reads it, the teacher trains against an ambient 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) prior with centre-of-mass augmentation on the data. Its own network removes the mean from input and output, so what it supplies downstream is the mean-free component of the velocity. Its optimizer settings, step count, and per-step cost are given alongside the flow-map phases that follow it, in Tab. 13 (“Velocity, phase 1”), Tab. 16 , and Tab. 17 respectively, since its own recorded wall-clock is what the flow-map training budget below is computed from. sections.heading: FALCON, FALCON-A, F2D2 and SCALLOP.
sections.text: We follow the original papers for the architecture and optimizer hyperparameters of these four flow-map baselines (FALCON/FALCON-A: Rehman et al. (2026a) ; F2D2: Ai et al. (2026) ; SCALLOP: OuYang et al. (2026) ). All four continue from the velocity teacher described above, through a two-phase pipeline : flow-map pretraining (Phase 1.5) and the distillation objective itself (Phase 2). Each phase frozen before the next one reads it. The original FALCON paper does not use a pretrain-then-distill procedure; we adopt it uniformly across all four baselines for consistency with F2D2 and SCALLOP, and since it starts from an independently pretrained velocity field, it can only match or improve on FALCON’s original recipe. The flow map itself extends the teacher’s time convention: X ⁡ ( x t , t , s ) = x t + ( s − t ) ​ u θ ​ ( x t , t , s ) X(x_{t},t,s)=x_{t}+(s-t)\,u_{\theta}(x_{t},t,s) with s < t s<t . All three papers run the opposite direction; each identity below is the reversal of the printed one, and each is invariant under it. Phase 1.5 — flow-map pretraining. One self-consistency identity for the average-velocity map u θ ​ ( x t , t , s ) u_{\theta}(x_{t},t,s) , trained against the frozen teacher on the same single-head backbone Phase 2 uses. Two objectives, neither of them new mathematics: • ESD (Eulerian), the MeanFlow identity u θ = v + ( s − t ) ​ ( v ⋅ ∇ x u θ + ∂ t u θ ) u_{\theta}=v+(s-t)\,(v\cdot\nabla_{x}u_{\theta}+\partial_{t}u_{\theta}) , which is FALCON’s average-velocity term standing alone; • LSD (Lagrangian), u θ ​ ( x t , t , s ) + ( s − t ) ​ ∂ s u θ ​ ( x t , t , s ) = sg ⁡ [ u θ ] ​ ( x s , s , s ) u_{\theta}(x_{t},t,s)+(s-t)\,\partial_{s}u_{\theta}(x_{t},t,s)=\mathrm{sg}[u_{\theta}](x_{s},s,s) at the mapped point x s x_{s} , which is F2D2’s and SCALLOP’s shared self-distillation term with no divergence head attached. We encourage to look at Boffi et al. (2025) for more details. ESD warm-starts FALCON and FALCON-A, LSD warm-starts F2D2 and SCALLOP, so there are two pretraining runs per system rather than four. The student loads the pretraining checkpoint’s EMA weights only: fresh optimizer, fresh schedule, step counter back to zero. For F2D2/SCALLOP the single-head parameters are remapped onto the dual-head layout (blocks → \to trunk, head → \to velocity head) and the divergence head is left at its zero initialization. Phase 2 — distillation. The four methods proper, on the single-head backbone (FALCON, FALCON-A) or the dual-head backbone with its separate divergence-readout head (F2D2, SCALLOP); Tab. 12 gives the sizes. Tab. 13 gives the optimizer settings of all three phases and Tables 14 and 15 the per-objective loss hyperparameters. The teacher enters phase 2 in three places: it is the regression target of the instantaneous/diagonal term, the tangent of the average-velocity JVP (FALCON, ESD), and the field whose divergence F2D2 estimates. Common to every phase. The whole problem is posed in the mean-free subspace so the map transports the centroid by the identity. Both times reach the network through a Fourier embedding of raw t t . F2D2, SCALLOP and LSD condition on the anchor and the step s − t s-t ; FALCON, FALCON-A and ESD on the two times independently, as MeanFlow ( Geng et al., 2025 ) does. The choice has to agree across a warm start, which is why the pretraining rows match the students they initialize. Training runs under bf16 mixed precision but the log-density accumulator is in fp32. Each phase keeps an EMA of decay 0.999 0.999 and skips the optimizer step on a non-finite loss or gradient norm. Chignolin trains 4-way DDP at the same global batch of 1024, every other system on a single GPU.

sections.heading: Training budget.
sections.text: OuYang et al. (2026, Appendix C.1) reports a budget of 4 × 10 6 4{\times}10^{6} update steps at batch 1000, but this figure is inconsistent with the paper’s own wall-clock numbers: at our measured per-step time on our GPU class, the reported step count would take an order of magnitude longer than the ∼ \sim 7–8 h the paper reports for its two phases combined. We therefore size the pipeline by wall-clock instead: the whole of it (all three phases) is given the recorded training time of the NF 2 M actually selected for that system ( Tab. 10 ). Tab. 17 gives all three quantities and Tab. 16 the resulting step counts. Matching time is not matching capacity or data: these backbones are 4.1M (single-head) and 6.1M (dual-head) parameters on the ALA systems against 18–87M for the NF 2 M flows, so a flow-map step is much cheaper and a time-matched pipeline takes many more of them. Summed over the three phases, the baselines see 2.7–9.0 × \times the number of passes over the training set that NF 2 M’s own 1000 epochs give.

sections.heading: Departures from a literal reading of the papers.
sections.text: Of the three, only Ai et al. (2026) released code, and the molecular code the F2D2/SCALLOP comparison is reproduced from isn’t available. Where code and paper disagree, we follow the code; where a value is left unstated, we flag our choice as unswept. The departures below fall into three kinds: the released code overriding a paper’s written equation, a stability or correctness fix we made and verified against a diagnostic (synthetic or molecular), and a value neither paper states at all. Code overrides the papers’ prose. • Self-distillation stop-gradient (F2D2, SCALLOP). Both papers write the correction term with the whole derivative detached. The released code detaches only the divergence-head correction and lets the velocity term’s derivative backpropagate. The literal, fully-detached version is unstable in our hands: on our synthetic diagnostic, the weight norm drifts unboundedly until a batch produces | x s | ∼ 10 10 |x_{s}|\!\sim\!10^{10} and training diverges. • Time-pair sampling. SCALLOP’s prose restricts ( s , t ) (s,t) to the upper triangle, but the F2D2 code samples both independently and uniformly over the full square and its own inverse sampler at evaluation time relies on having seen the reversed ordering during training. We sample the full square for all six objectives, so every pretraining checkpoint covers the same measure as the student that reads it. • Divergence head and target scale (F2D2). SCALLOP’s stated contribution is a vectorized divergence head (F2D2’s released code has a scalar one). Vectorizing F2D2 looks at first like a free upgrade so we did it. Targets are then scaled by the reference’s own head-shape rule ( ∇ ⁣ ⋅ ⁡ 1 \divergence 1 vectorized, ∇ ⁣ ⋅ ⁡ d \divergence d scalar) rather than the factor of 10 transcribed from the papers’ 2D toy, which has no molecular support: their other published anchor is ∼ 10 4 {\sim}10^{4} at d = 12288 d=12288 , four orders away, with the peptides ( d = 66 d=66 – 414 414 ) in between. Stability and correctness fixes. They were all obtained by doing ablations on synthetic or molecular targets. • Unsigned average-velocity head (FALCON). The paper’s u θ = sign ⁡ ( t − s ) ​ h θ u_{\theta}=\mathrm{sign}(t-s)\,h_{\theta} forces h θ h_{\theta} to jump by 2 ​ v 2v at the diagonal, so only the branch the tie-forcing sits on ever learns the correct side; we leave the head unsigned. • Stopped average-velocity derivative. Left live, as in the reference, the residual becomes second-order in the network for both FALCON’s L avg L_{\mathrm{avg}} and the ESD identity, since prediction and target come out of the same JVP call. We stop it. • Floored, projected SCALLOP divergence target. 1 / σ t 1/\sigma_{t} with σ t = t \sigma_{t}=t reaches 10 4 10^{4} near the data end, so a single sample would dominate the batch; we floor it at 10 − 3 10^{-3} , at the cost of a small bias over the innermost decade of times, and state the target in the mean-free subspace rather than the ambient one. • FALCON-A’s sub-jump weights. The paper prints the two shares swapped relative to the identity’s own derivative; they only agree at the paper’s fixed λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 , which is why the error never surfaces in its results. • SCALLOP’s loss-uncertainty weighting. Implemented but left off: as specified, exp ⁡ ( − ψ ) ​ L + ψ \exp(-\psi)L+\psi is unbounded below wherever the (self-distillation) loss it weights can reach zero, stationary at ψ = log ⁡ L \psi=\log L with value 1 + log ⁡ L 1+\log L . Clamping ψ \psi bounds the weight but not the outcome; we found no stated fix and record this as an open parity gap rather than paper over it. Left unstated by both papers. • Diagonal batch share. 0.75 0.75 for FALCON/ESD (MeanFlow’s ( Geng et al., 2025 ) own ratio, the only published value for an average-velocity objective) and 0.5 0.5 for the Lagrangian family (the complement of F2D2’s stated self-distillation split). Never swept. • Chignolin’s flow-map backbone and NFE. Neither paper reports chignolin; both are extrapolated with the same channel/block-doubling rule already used for the DiT presets ( Tab. 11 ), giving the backbone in Tab. 12 and the step count in Tab. 20 . sections.heading: NF 2 M.
sections.text: Both NF 2 M-IS and NF 2 M-MIS sample a checkpoint from Tab. 10 , using the time grid of ( Karras et al., 2022 ) with ρ = 7 \rho=7 , run in bf16 precision with N = 10,000 N=10{,}000 particles. Shared initialization of multiple trajectories. At terminal noise, X T X_{T} and X 0 X_{0} are nearly independent, so p 0 | T ≈ p 0 p_{0|T}\approx p_{0} : the first denoising kernel, from t K t_{K} to t K − 1 t_{K-1} , is essentially independent of the value of x T x_{T} . We exploit this when drawing N N trajectories in parallel: rather than sampling N N independent terminal states x T n ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ T 2 ​ I ) x_{T}^{n}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{T}^{2}I) and running N N separate SNIS corrections ( 12 ) with M M particles each, we draw a single x T x_{T} and build one SNIS approximation with N ​ M NM candidates, which we then reuse by sampling from it N N times. Since p 0 | T ≈ p 0 p_{0|T}\approx p_{0} means the denoising posterior at this step is as hard to approximate as the target itself, pooling all N ​ M NM candidates concentrates statistical power precisely where the conditional flow q 0 | t θ q^{\theta}_{0|t} faces its hardest task. This sharing introduces a slight correlation between the N N trajectories, which were otherwise independent; the correlation stays weak, however, precisely because the denoising kernel depends only weakly on x T x_{T} at this step. Candidate budget. For NF 2 M-IS, the candidate count M M is solved per (system, variant, K K ) for the largest value whose measured wall-clock matches the corresponding unconditional baseline’s own wall-clock; the selected checkpoints use the values in Tab. 18 . For NF 2 M-MIS, the architecture is fixed to the single variant with the best validation NF 2 M-IS score at K = 8 K=8 per system ( Tab. 10 , MIS row); the values of M M and the mixture size are given in Tab. 19 . sections.heading: Velocity teacher.
sections.text: The phase-1 velocity field is also evaluated on its own, as a flow-matching baseline in the style of ECNF++ ( Tan et al., 2025 ) , on the same protocol as everything else so its row sits beside theirs. Samples are the probability-flow ODE’s push-forward of an ambient 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) prior, integrated from the prior end down to the data end by adaptive Dormand–Prince at rtol = atol = 10 − 4 \texttt{rtol}=\texttt{atol}=10^{-4} with the data end inset at t min = 10 − 5 t_{\min}=10^{-5} , where the linear schedule is singular. That comes to roughly 130–165 function evaluations per solve. The log-density is the instantaneous change of variables accumulated along the same trajectory, with the exact divergence: one JVP per input coordinate, d = 66 d=66 – 414 414 . There is no probe count to tune. This run is fp32 rather than bf16: the log-determinant is an integral accumulated over ∼ 160 {\sim}160 solver steps and is the whole point of the evaluation. We use N = 10 4 N=10^{4} proposals per seed over 3 seeds then post-hoc MALA chain as every other method to match the energy evaluation budget (see Tab. 25 ). 10 4 10^{4} rather than the 10 6 10^{6} the flow-map and TarFlow cells use is what the exact likelihood affords .

sections.heading: FALCON, FALCON-A, F2D2 and SCALLOP.
sections.text: All four sample the phase-2 checkpoint at its EMA weights, at a fixed per-system number of flow-map steps ( Tab. 20 ), in bf16 with the prior, the log-determinant, and the log-density accumulator held in fp32. FALCON and FALCON-A step on FALCON’s own EDM-shaped grid ( σ min = 10 − 3 \sigma_{\min}=10^{-3} , σ max = 1 \sigma_{\max}=1 , ρ = 7 \rho=7 , mapped affinely onto [ 10 − 4 , 1 − 10 − 4 ] [10^{-4},1-10^{-4}] , which puts the fine steps at the data end); F2D2 and SCALLOP on the uniform grid in t t that their paper states. Density evaluation. The two families read their density differently, and the difference is what the evaluation costs. FALCON and FALCON-A have no divergence head, so log ⁡ q \log q is a sum of per-step Jacobian log-determinants, a dense d × d d\times d Jacobian per step, evaluated in fp32 whatever precision the network itself ran in, since a determinant amplifies rounding error with matrix size. F2D2 and SCALLOP read their divergence head and accumulate ∑ i ( s i − t i ) ​ ∑ j D θ ​ ( x t i , t i , s i ) j \sum_{i}(s_{i}-t_{i})\sum_{j}D_{\theta}(x_{t_{i}},t_{i},s_{i})_{j} . Evaluation protocol. Evaluation is self-normalized importance sampling against the Boltzmann target, with 10 6 10^{6} proposals per seed over 3 seeds, scored on the test split. The one exception is FALCON and FALCON-A on chignolin, where the exact per-step Jacobian costs ∼ 500 {\sim}500 GPU-hours per seed at 10 6 10^{6} proposals, and the pool is 10 5 10^{5} instead. Importance weights are computed on the original proposals using their proposal densities and Boltzmann energies. We then resample 10 4 10^{4} configurations according to the normalized weights and apply post-hoc MALA steps to each selected configuration (see Tab. 25 for the number of steps). The refined configurations retain equal weights, with no post-MALA importance-weight computation, and are compared against 10 4 10^{4} reference configurations. A MALA kernel that leaves the Boltzmann target invariant can be applied before resampling while retaining the pre-move importance weights, or after resampling while retaining equal weights. Both constructions preserve the target in the importance-sampling limit, although their finite-sample dependence and variance can differ. The unconditional SNIS baseline follows the same order. No centre-of-mass correction is applied, unlike the TarFlow/StarFlow baselines: these models are mean-free end to end and no centre-of-mass augmentation enters their training, so their proposal density carries no centroid factor to correct. The teacher itself is a strong sampler in its own right (competitive with the global comparison of Tab. 1 ) and on ALA-2 it beats all four flow maps outright. On the larger systems the picture is mixed rather than uniformly closing: it is specifically the single-head family, FALCON and FALCON-A, that occasionally overtakes the teacher, while the dual-head family essentially never does. Since the teacher is already a competitive sampler, these occasional wins are not evidence that it was undertrained. The inference-time column looks paradoxical: the flow maps draw 100 × 100\times more particles than the teacher ( 10 6 10^{6} against 10 4 10^{4} as 10 6 10^{6} was unfeasible with the velocity teacher) while taking roughly 10 × 10\times fewer steps (4–16 NFE against ∼ \sim 130–165, Tab. 20 ). For FALCON and FALCON-A these two factors largely cancel: their dense d × d d\times d Jacobian log-determinant, paid at every step, erases the step-count saving, leaving wall-clock inference never faster than the teacher and up to 6.3 × 6.3\times slower on ALA-6. F2D2 and SCALLOP avoid that cost by reading a divergence head instead, so the step-count saving survives the extra particles: both are consistently 19 19 – 22 × 22\times faster than the teacher across all four systems.

sections.heading: Cost of the Langevin refinements.
sections.text: Every sampler reported here spends part of its inference budget on Langevin dynamics, and at a matched target-energy budget the two kernels enter at the same scale. NF 2 M pays both: 512 MAExL steps at every level, over the full particle set, plus 128 steps of post-hoc MALA on its (comparatively small) returned sample. Every other method pays only the post-hoc chain, but at the step count that equalises the budget ( Tab. 25 ). Tab. 23 gives the measured wall-clock and its share of each sampler’s inference time. With refinement, NF 2 M is best in energy on every system except ALA-6, and best in torsion on ALA-6 and chignolin. Without it, NF 2 M is best in energy on every system and in torsion on the three largest. Its own numbers barely depend on the ladder: torsion is unchanged to within 0.001 0.001 and energy moves by small amounts in both directions. The baselines behave in the opposite way. Most of their energy accuracy comes from the ladder, their raw distances are up to an order of magnitude worse on the larger systems, and for several of them the raw seed standard deviation is comparable to the mean. FALCON’s refined energy win on ALA-6 in particular does not survive: its raw distance is more than twice that of NF 2 M-IS, even though FALCON runs over a hundred times longer. In torsion space, the ladder improves the baselines by at most about 15 % 15\% and leaves their order unchanged, so the shape of that comparison is a property of the proposals themselves.

sections.heading: Matching the target-energy budget.
sections.text: Figure 8: Energy Wasserstein distance against the matched target-energy budget, on the four ALA systems and chignolin. Every point on a panel spends the same number of target-energy calls. The three budgets are the 0-, 512- and 1024-MAExL-step settings of Tab. 4 for NF 2 M, and the equalizing post-hoc MALA ladders of Tab. 25 for the SNIS-based samplers. Means over three seeds. Figure 9: Torus Wasserstein distance against the matched target-energy budget, same protocol and seeds as Fig. 8 . Figure 10: Inference wall-clock against the matched target-energy budget, same protocol and seeds as Fig. 8 . FALCON and FALCON-A are omitted, their per-step Jacobian log-determinant putting them off the scale of every panel. Table 25: Number of post-hoc MALA steps run for the SNIS-based samplers at each matched budget. Each step count is chosen so that the SNIS-based total, P P energy calls for the importance weights plus n ⁡ ( S + 1 ) n\,(S+1) score calls on n = 10 4 n=10^{4} chains with one score call counted as two energy calls, matches the budget of the corresponding NF 2 M setting. All SNIS-based samplers use P = 10 6 P=10^{6} proposals, except FALCON and FALCON-A on chignolin, which use P = 10 5 P=10^{5} and therefore take longer ladders for the same total. MAExL steps System Methods 0 512 1024 ALA-2 ( d = 66 d=66 ) SNIS, FALCON, FALCON-A, F2D2, SCALLOP 114 4212 8308 ALA-3 ( d = 99 d=99 ) 127 4231 8327 ALA-4 ( d = 126 d=126 ) 135 4239 8335 ALA-6 ( d = 189 d=189 ) 134 4238 8334 Chignolin ( d = 414 d=414 ) SNIS, F2D2, SCALLOP 129 4228 8324 FALCON, FALCON-A 174 4273 8369 ALA-2 ( d = 66 d=66 ) Velocity teacher 163 4261 8357 ALA-3 ( d = 99 d=99 ) 176 4280 8376 ALA-4 ( d = 126 d=126 ) 184 4288 8384 ALA-6 ( d = 189 d=189 ) 183 4287 8383 Since MAExL and the post-hoc ladder both query the target, wall-clock alone does not settle whether NF 2 M simply spends more energy evaluations than the baselines. We therefore equalize the count exactly at three operating points, one per MAExL setting of Tab. 4 , re-polishing every SNIS-based sampler from its unrefined samples with the ladder length that spends the same number of target-energy calls, counting a score as two. Tab. 25 gives those lengths, and Figs. 8 , 9 and 10 trace every method across the three budgets. The leftmost point handicaps NF 2 M, since matching it means running with no MAExL at all, precisely the setting the ablation identifies as its weakest, while the baselines lose little from a shortened chain. From the middle budget onward NF 2 M recovers its Tab. 1 numbers and with them the ranking of the main table, whereas the extra calls granted to the baselines buy energy accuracy only: their torsion curves are close to flat and stay well behind on the larger systems, since a local kernel cannot redistribute mass between torsional metastable states however long it runs. The one place the verdict shifts is chignolin energy at the largest budget, where several baselines become indistinguishable from NF 2 M in the mean, though their across-seed spread remains far wider. Matching energy calls also does not equalize wall-clock, and the gap widens with the budget, since a longer ladder is pure serial cost for the baselines while NF 2 M pays its share inside the sampling loop. The conclusion of the main table is therefore unchanged: the separation lies in the proposal rather than in the refinement budget.

The two methods trade places depending on the regime. On the smallest peptides, the geometric annealing path is clearly beneficial in torsion space, where SBG-SMC is the strongest baseline, while NF 2 M already dominates in energy space. This ordering reverses as the dimension grows: on the largest systems NF 2 M improves on the best SBG-SMC variant on both metrics, and the gap is widest on chignolin, where the SMC ladder degrades sharply. Two further properties separate the methods. First, SBG-SMC is markedly less stable, both across seeds, with several runs whose standard deviation is of the order of their mean, whereas NF 2 M varies little across seeds and across its two importance-sampling variants. Second, at an equal proposal budget the annealing ladder roughly doubles inference time on the ALA systems and costs several times more on chignolin, for comparable training cost. Finally, since SNIS and SBG-SMC use the same unconditional checkpoints and differ only at inference, their comparison isolates the effect of the annealing path itself. Although the two use different proposal budgets for a comparable wall-clock, the picture matches the ablation of Tan et al. (2025) , the ladder helping on some systems and hurting on others rather than yielding a consistent gain.

Boltzmann Generators address this by pairing a generative model with importance sampling to obtain consistent samples from the target distribution. We introduce Normalizing Flow Flow Maps (NF 2 M), which combines the strengths of recent stochastic flow maps with the tractability of classic normalizing flows to build a Boltzmann Generator. Unlike most methods, which correct the generative model only at the end, NF 2 M reweighs each denoising transition as generation proceeds, avoiding wasted compute on trajectories that are ultimately discarded. At each denoising step, a conditional normalizing flow proposes clean configurations given the current noisy state (a simpler task than sampling directly from the target) and its exact likelihood enables correcting each proposal toward the true denoising transition of the target Boltzmann distribution. This is in contrast to most existing methods, whose likelihoods are approximate or expensive to evaluate, undermining the statistical reliability of the correction. We establish consistency of the corrected transitions and bound how approximation errors propagate through the sampling chain. We evaluate NF 2 M on peptide systems, demonstrating improved sampling efficiency and sample quality. 1 Introduction Sampling the Boltzmann distribution of molecular systems is central to statistical physics, underlying protein folding, ligand binding, conformational change, and molecular design ( Liu, 2001 ; Frenkel and Smit, 2001 ; Noé et al., 2009 ; Lindorff-Larsen et al., 2011 ; Buch et al., 2011 ) . This remains hard because molecular energy landscapes are high-dimensional and rugged, with metastable states separated by large barriers. Classical approaches like MD and MCMC are asymptotically exact ( Leimkuhler and Matthews, 2015 ; Frenkel and Smit, 2001 ; Wirnsberger et al., 2020 ) , but their local-update nature makes them mix slowly on such landscapes, producing correlated samples and requiring prohibitively long runs to capture transitions between metastable states. Boltzmann Generators (BGs) take a different strategy ( Noé et al., 2019 ; Müller et al., 2019 ) : a learned generative model produces plausible configurations independently and in parallel, which are then statistically corrected toward the true equilibrium distribution, e.g. via importance sampling (IS). This hinges on two requirements: proposal-target overlap and a tractable correction procedure—that existing generative backbones trade off differently. Normalizing flows (NFs) ( Rezende and Mohamed, 2015 ; Dinh et al., 2017 ; Noé et al., 2019 ; Papamakarios et al., 2021 ) dominate this role because their tractable likelihoods enable IS correction, but their invertibility constraints limit expressiveness and overlap. Bridging the NF to target gap via temperature-annealed interpolation ( Tan et al., 2025 ) instead suffers from mass teleportation on multimodal targets ( Woodard et al., 2009 ; Máté and Fleuret, 2023 ) and does not reliably outperform direct importance sampling ( Tan et al., 2025 ) . Continuous normalizing flows built from ODE trajectories ( Chen et al., 2018 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ) offer more expressive architectures, but their likelihoods require integrating the vector-field divergence, making correction costly and discretization-sensitive. Distilling these into few-step flow maps ( Boffi et al., 2025 ) sacrifices tractable likelihoods altogether. Subsequent work restores likelihoods for such few-step maps in two ways : FALCON ( Rehman et al., 2026a ) computes them from the full Jacobian of the map, at the cost of memory overhead and sensitivity to the map’s numerical invertibility, while F2D2 ( Ai et al., 2026 ) and SCALLOP ( OuYang et al., 2026 ) instead distill a likelihood-prediction head, gaining speed but risking error propagation from the learned likelihood into the correction step. Diffusion models offer a different stochastic transport path, gradually perturbing clean samples via a tractable noising process and generating through learned, typically Gaussian, denoising transitions ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) . These paths handle multimodal targets better than temperature annealing and have shown promise for BGs ( Grenioux and Noble, 2026 ) : although the endpoint density is intractable, the path density can be evaluated, enabling correction in an extended space ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . The Gaussian approximation is accurate only for fine discretizations, however, creating a tradeoff between statistical performance and inference cost ( Grenioux and Noble, 2026 ) . Distributional diffusion and stochastic flow maps address this by modeling the full conditional distribution of clean samples given a noisy state, enabling expressive transitions over larger stepsizes ( De Bortoli et al., 2025 ; Potaptchik et al., 2026 ; Holderrieth et al., 2026 ) but the resulting models are typically implicit, lacking the likelihoods BG correction needs. We close this gap with Normalizing Flow Flow Maps (NF 2 M), a BG that generates samples along a diffusion transport path in a few steps using denoising kernels estimated via importance sampling. Like stochastic flow maps, NF 2 M models the conditional distribution q θ ​ ( x 0 | x t ) q^{\theta}(x_{0}|x_{t}) of clean data given a noisy state, but it uses a conditional NF rather than an implicit model, yielding a tractable density. This tractability lets us build an importance-sampling estimator of the true denoising kernel, exact as the number of particles grows: at each step, we propose candidates from q θ ​ ( x 0 | x t ) q^{\theta}(x_{0}|x_{t}) and reweight them against the tractable conditional target p ⁡ ( x 0 | x t ) p(x_{0}|x_{t}) (which is the product of the Boltzmann density and the diffusion noising kernel) yielding a Rao-Blackwellized mixture estimator that we sample to denoise the current state. Iterating this gradually transports noise toward the Boltzmann target, unlike NF- and CNF-based BGs that bridge the gap in one step. By stochastic localization ( Grenioux et al., 2024 ) , p ⁡ ( x 0 | x t ) p(x_{0}|x_{t}) loses its multimodality and concentrates as t → 0 t\to 0 which makes it easier to sample from and simplifies the conditional NF’s approximation target. Our main contributions are: • We propose Normalizing Flow Flow Maps (NF 2 M), a Boltzmann Generator that parameterizes a stochastic flow map with a normalizing flow, combining tractable densities with few-step generation. • We design novel conditional normalizing flow architectures for molecule generation, adapting state-of-the-art image and video normalizing flows to this setting ( Zhai et al., 2025 ; Gu et al., 2026 ) . • We propose two inference strategies, NF 2 M-IS and NF 2 M-MIS, that yield asymptotically exact samples from the Boltzmann distribution, and support them with theoretical guarantees. • We evaluate NF 2 M against NF and flow-map baselines across molecular systems of varying sizes, demonstrating competitive or superior performance. 2 Background Problem setup. Sequential Boltzmann Generators (SBG) use sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) to sample along a geometric annealing path between a trained TarFlow proposal and the Boltzmann target. However, their ablation results show that SMC does not consistently improve over SNIS on the same trained proposal across systems and metrics ( Tan et al., 2025 ) . NF 2 M also deploys a TarFlow sequentially, but both inference and learning differ fundamentally: rather than annealing a fixed proposal toward the target, NF 2 M performs progressive denoising transitions, and the flow itself is trained as a conditional model rather than an unconditional one. The Autoregressive Boltzmann Generator (ArBG) models coordinate-bin probabilities with uniform dequantization ( Rehman et al., 2026b ) , yielding an exactly evaluable but bin-wise coarse density. Its coordinate-wise factorization enables twisted SMC using temporarily capped peptide energies to resample partial structures. Stochastic normalizing flows interleave invertible maps with MCMC or Langevin transitions, weighting entire sampling paths ( Wu et al., 2020 ) . NF 2 M instead corrects denoising proposals over complete molecular configurations at each noise level, avoiding both the binning artifacts of ArBG and the need to evaluate energies of artificially capped partial structures. BGs with approximate correction. Free-form Flows jointly train a network and its pseudo-inverse by maximum likelihood ( Draxler et al., 2024 ) . Continuous normalizing flows keep maximum-likelihood training but replace the invertible network with a neural ODE ( Köhler et al., 2020 ) , whose likelihood requires integrating the costly probability-flow ODE through the network’s divergence, with many steps needed for both accuracy and invertibility. Later work cuts training cost via flow matching but leaves this inference cost untouched ( Klein et al., 2023b ; Klein and Noé, 2024 ) . FALCON instead distills into a few-step flow map, replacing the full ODE integration with a handful of Jacobian evaluations, at the price of only approximate invertibility ( Rehman et al., 2026a ) . F2D2 drops exact Jacobians entirely, jointly distilling the flow map and its density evolution via Hutchinson trace estimates ( Ai et al., 2026 ; Hutchinson, 1990 ) , and SCALLOP replaces this with a Hutchinson-free conditional divergence-matching loss ( OuYang et al., 2026 ) . Across these distillation-based methods, the learned density’s approximation error enters the importance weights directly and persists regardless of proposal count. NF 2 M instead evaluates its conditional proposal densities exactly. Stochastic flow maps and intermediate correction. Distributional diffusion models learn the conditional distribution of clean states given noisy states, enabling larger denoising steps ( Xiao et al., 2022 ; De Bortoli et al., 2025 ) . Meta Flow Maps and Diamond Maps use clean-state candidates for intermediate correction toward reward-tilted distributions ( Potaptchik et al., 2026 ; Holderrieth et al., 2026 ) . Their implicit conditional generators do not directly provide the proposal densities needed for Boltzmann importance weights. NF 2 M supplies them through a conditional normalizing flow. 5 Experiments Benchmarks. We evaluate on the five all-atom peptide systems of Tan et al.
